# planetGen Roadmap

## How to use this document

This file tracks **open work only**. Finished work is not listed here:
`CHANGELOG.md` and git history are the record. For how things work today,
read the code and the reference docs (`src/stellarObjects/schema.sql` and
`docs/reference/database-schema.md` for the schema, `docs/reference/api.md` and
`docs/reference/html-interface.md` for the web interface,
`docs/design/galaxy/galaxy-coordinate-system.md` for galaxy geometry).

Each open item says what's wrong (the observed symptom), where to start
looking, and what "done" means, so it can be picked up cold. Items with
open questions for Boss state the default taken; the work can start on
that default.

### IDs

- Every item has an ID made of its category and a number, `CAT.N`, for
  example `MAP.16`. The number is a plain count within the category,
  like the database schema version: the first item in a category is
  `.1`, and each new item, subitem or bug takes the next number. There
  are no deeper levels (no `MAP.2.1`); an item's place in the tree is
  shown by indenting it under its parent, not by its ID. The categories
  are in the table below.
- IDs are permanent. Nothing is renumbered, and an ID is never reused.
  When an item ships, delete it here (the changelog is the record) and
  describe the change in the PR's `changes/` note; its ID stays taken. A
  finished item that still has open subitems stays as a checked line so
  its subitems keep their place.
- A new ID is one more than the highest ever issued in its category,
  finished items included.
  [plan/todo-number-map.md](plan/todo-number-map.md) lists every ID
  issued so far and the next free number in each category. It also maps
  the old running numbers (1 to 111, used until 2026-10-01 in the
  changelog, commits, PR titles and older docs) and the dotted tree IDs
  used briefly on 2026-10-01 (such as `MAP.2.1.1`, in PRs #189 and
  #190) to these IDs.

### Where new work goes

- A new feature is a new item, or a subitem (indented under the item it
  extends, with its own next number).
- A bug is a subitem of the item whose feature it breaks, marked
  "(bug)". A bug in something with no item here is a top-level item in
  its category, marked "(bug)" (for example UX.15).
- Everything Boss reports from live observation of the running app is a
  bug, never a feature or an enhancement (Boss, 8:44 PM EDT 2026-10-22):
  file it as a bug item marked "(bug)", whatever the wording (a layout
  note, a name, a missing control, a slow stage, an implausible number).
- The project is in early alpha (Boss, 2026-10-15 5:27 PM EDT): the
  current database schema is not a constraint on any item. Redesign
  tables, columns and layouts as the work needs, with one migration or a
  fresh galaxy.

### Sources and stand-ins (Boss, 8:16 PM EDT 2026-10-29, full build in 8.1)

- Physics found in research still wins: a primary source that has been
  read beats everything below it.
- A secondary source (a paper that cites a paper, a review, a table in
  another work) is accepted by default. Hand-tuning is the alternative
  when nothing is built, so a secondary value is better than a tweak.
  Label it 2ND-HAND in the registry row and name the citing work; if the
  primary is read later, the primary replaces it.
- A stand-in is fine where a value is needed and no source gives it, as
  long as it is indexed and registered in the stand-in registry (GEN.725)
  with its tier and tweak level (L0 to L4), so later research can replace
  it. An unregistered constant is the only thing not allowed.
- This relaxes how strictly a thing must be sourced before it is built,
  not how stable the generator must be. The earlier rules still hold:
  verified wins over unverified, two verified sources in doubt means the
  newest, two in question means the widest range, nothing fixed from the
  Solar System or the Milky Way.
- Where an older item says a source must be verified first, that a
  stand-in is not allowed, or that a physics piece waits for a version
  after 8.1, the newer rule wins and the item is read with this change.

### Investigation log

- Every test or investigation on an item gets a dated comment on its goal issue, whether it fixes, fails or cannot reproduce (Boss, 2026-10-16,
  11:48 PM EDT: "I want to keep issues having a running history of what we do and why"). A bug that could not be reproduced, or that needs
  more information, is flagged so in the item (a "Status" line) and in a comment headed with the item ID and the words "Could not reproduce"
  or "Needs information", giving the date and time in EDT, what was run (the number of runs, the load, the inputs), the result, and the
  failure text needed next time. The comment is the history; the item says only the latest status.

### Links

- This file is the only place that links an item to its design document,
  on its own line under the item:
  `Design: [docs/design/x.md](design/x.md), section N`. Design documents
  don't list item IDs.
- The version files in [plan/](plan/) are the other place that lists
  item IDs: each version file has a table of its items per thread and
  phase (see "Plan: versions" below). File a new item into one thread's
  table of one phase in the same PR, and delete its row when it ships.
- Code tags cite the ID: `TODO(MAP.16): what to do here`. Grep
  `"TODO(MAP."` for an area, or `"TODO(MAP.16)"` for one item.
- `changes/` notes, PR titles and commit messages cite the ID, for
  example "Galaxy Map: stages (MAP.16)".

### Categories

| ID | Covers |
|---|---|
| UX | Web pages, the site shell, menus, page content |
| MAP | Galaxy Map, Sector Map, System Map |
| NAV | Navigation and travel (NAV page, courses, speeds) |
| GEN | Generation and physics (stars, systems, phenomena, galaxy model) |
| PERF | Speed, caching, bulk generation and parallel work |
| DB | Schema and migrations |
| API | The JSON API |
| ADM | Admin tools: editing, overrides, Generate page |
| SEC | Security |
| TEST | The test suite itself: new tests, test infrastructure, CI test jobs |
| USR | User accounts |
| OPS | Installers, hosting, CI, releases |
| DOC | Documentation and project process |
| VIEW | The view from a planet |
| POP | Population and politics |

## Background

The long-term goal is a fully populated galaxy (every sector, system,
planet, moon and belt) stored in MySQL and browsed through a web
interface served from Apache. The original roadmap phases are all done:
object-graph serialization, the relational schema and migrations, CLI
tools writing to the database, lazy galaxy-scale generation from a
density skeleton, and the Flask API (`src/html/api/`) with server-rendered
pages served by the same app (`src/html/web/`): Galaxy, Sector and System
maps, search, NAV, admin auth and wiki publishing.

## UX: Web pages

Boss's UX reference for this section is "Responsive Web Design
Standards" (Boss's notes of 2026-10-01; a copy is in the project's
shared files at `ux-standards/`). The rules from it that apply here:
size classes by width (compact under 600 px, medium 600-839, expanded
840-1199, desktop 1200+), not by device; viewport media queries only for
the top-level frame and container queries for everything inside it; on
medium and wider screens a menu must not stretch across the screen like a
phone's; text columns capped at 45-75 characters, but a map or canvas may
use the full width; touch targets at least 44-48 px on coarse pointers
(`pointer: coarse`), smaller is fine for a mouse; spacing and type sized
with `clamp()`.

- [ ] **MAP.171 The Galaxy Map keys a massive phenomenon's visibility to its map luminosity (replaces "always lit")**
  Boss (2026-10-10 21:38Z): "inject into the phenomena part of that, use
  the following mass/luminosity to allow us to store a 'map visibility'
  value for phenomena that aren't bright but have large mass. The idea
  being that a neutron star of say 2 solar masses should be given
  placement on the map when a star's brightness at 2 solar masses would
  be visible. Same for black holes, if a super massive black hole has a
  mass well above the brightest star, then it's visibility on the map
  should be keyed to that. This allows us to put items on the map that
  aren't bright enough to be seen but are of importance (major
  gravitational locations are always important to navigation)." Today
  the client law (MAP.148, built in PR #1160) gives black holes, neutron
  stars and quasars a fixed magnitude (PHENOMENON_MAGNITUDE = -40 in
  starmagnitude.js), so they stay lit at any distance, and the
  400-per-tile cap and the server floors treat them separately. Done:
  the tile carries the map luminosity of each phenomenon (in the wire
  format of MAP.157/158/161 and the packed tiles of MAP.159, as one more
  plane or field), the client turns it into an apparent magnitude
  exactly as for a star, so a 2 Msun neutron star appears when a 2 Msun
  star (about 17 Lsun) would, and a supermassive black hole far above
  the brightest star stays visible across the galaxy; the server's
  per-tile choice ranks phenomena and stars together by luminosity or
  map luminosity, so the 400 cap and the generated_star_floor_sol floors
  treat them alike. Colours stay as MAP.164 (black holes purple, neutron
  stars dark blue) and sizes as MAP.165 (by mass). Overlap: MAP.152 owns
  the distance-cut tile choice, the floor removal and the cap
  reconciliation in the same query, so this item follows MAP.152 and
  uses its tile choice. Not a prerequisite of the 8.1 headline
  (MAP.146). Owner: Foundations lane 2, queued right after MAP.152.
  Prerequisites: none. Related: MAP.148,
  MAP.164, MAP.165, MAP.159, MAP.146.
  Status (2026-10-09): DB.24 done (Foundations lane 1, 2026-10-14,
  #1317, schema v83): nebula_field holds every kept class M and N cloud,
  written by plan from the seed. Deviation: rows carry no object id
  until a sector stores the cloud (an id needs a nebula shape, about 112
  ms each, roughly 30 CPU hours for all clouds at default scale); a save
  fills uid and is_stored (the flag is is_stored because 'stored' is
  reserved on MySQL 8), and plan links clouds a galaxy already holds.
  Key unstored clouds by (cell_i, cell_j, cell_k, n).
  Owner: Core 2 (Boss's lanes to 8.1, 2026-10-17, 10:06 AM EDT; lane
  assignment
  /mnt/project-files/reports/core1-5-lanes-to-8-1-2026-10-17.md). This replaces any earlier owner line on this item.

- [ ] **MAP.253 Map and scene read the parent chain: systemscene, body_positions, the browser twin orbitpositions.js and the systemmap branches drop the three origin conventions**
  Part of the unified orbited-body plan (GEN.550; design note
  docs/design/architecture/unified-system-barycentre.md, decided: Boss's nine cards
  on the System design, as the coordinator relayed with the wake times
  converted: S1, S2, S4, S5, S6, S7, S8 and S9 tapped between 12:10 and
  12:13 AM EDT on 2026-10-18, S3 at 12:15 AM EDT ('Most massive, pairs
  stay binary'), every one the recommended option: S1 a member's stored
  orbit is its barycentre about the central object (a planet's stored
  state is the barycentre of the planet and its moons), S2 the central
  object's offset is derived on read and never stored (the wobble
  columns go), S3 the most massive member is the central object and
  comparable-mass pairs stay binary nodes, S4 a system node takes a
  central child and any number of members, S5 a stand-in size cut of 1
  km diameter for hosting satellites plus fit and stability checks, S6
  moons may have satellites through the same gate with a tidal-survival
  gate row first (the odds start at zero; this supersedes 'moons are the
  lowest level'), S7 the point class's system frame measures from the
  top-level barycentre with a new local frame from the immediate
  parent's barycentre, S8 the stored values change in the 8.4 revision
  with DB.73 and DB.67 to DB.71, S9 a System is a view (rows with a
  common parent link, cached sums)). Boss's message of 12:03 AM EDT,
  2026-10-18 (project chat): a System is unified rules around the
  central object (as binary stars are done now); every object other than
  the central object can be another system with that object as its
  central object, down to small objects that get no satellites; all
  objects follow the same physics, so the origin of the system's space
  is the gravitational center and the central object may move around it.
  Item SY7 of the note. Proposed owner, not assigned by a card: Core 2
  for the browser and Core 4 for the Python. Do:

  wide binary conventions go. The Python and the JS must stay in step
  (`tests/test_js_unit.py` checks them against each other). Done: the
  system map draws the same scene and the Python and JS positions agree
  by test.
  Built code waiting for its caller (audit research, relayed 8:03 PM EDT
  2026-10-22 as the lane's clock reads): `physics/body_positions.py` is built and
  tested but no production Python imports it yet; this item is one of its planned callers. Boss (8:04 PM
  EDT): code built for a pending feature stays.

- [ ] **NAV.4 Save a course**

  no matter what they wanted in the first place." Today a course
  (`/nav?from=...&to=...`, `queryDb.nav_between`) can only be
  bookmarked as a URL. Done: a signed-in user can save a course under a
  name. A saved course always keeps both forms:
  - the direct, point-to-point line (its bearing and mark, NAV.1);
  - the system-to-system route (the chain of systems it hops through).
  The user can list, open, rename and delete their saved courses. The
  saved course shows whichever form the user views, and they can switch
  between the two. Needs user accounts (USR.1) and their storage.
  Question (decided below): until user accounts exist, should saving be
  admin-only, or
  per browser like bookmarks?
  Default taken for the open question (pre-planning thread): Default for
  the open question: per browser now (the same storage and menu as
  bookmarks), moved into the account when USR.7 lands. NAV.4 then does
  not wait for user accounts.

- [ ] **NAV.6 Courses that steer clear of gravity wells**
  Boss (2026-10-01 20:55Z): "we need to factor gravitational bodies into
  the course. A ship piloting would adjust the course to avoid falling
  into the gravitational field of objects it knows about. We'll need to
  have the system automatically adjust the course to avoid objects,
  attempting to stay out of the Hill sphere of each object. We're also
  going to use this within the sector and within the star system."
  Today a course is a straight line between its ends (NAV.1), and the
  route is a chain of systems. Done: course planning finds the bodies
  near the path that it knows about, and bends the path to stay outside
  each one's Hill sphere (or a safe radius where a Hill sphere doesn't
  apply, such as a star in the galaxy or a black hole). This works:
  - between systems in the galaxy (stars, black holes, neutron stars,
    nebulae and other phenomena);
  - inside a sector;
  - inside a star system (planets and moons, around the star).
  The adjusted path, its extra length and its time at each speed (NAV.2)
  are shown with the course, and the straight line stays available for
  comparison. Question (decided below): a Hill sphere needs an orbit
  around a
  heavier body, so what radius applies to a star or a lone object? And
  does the system level need the bodies' positions at a given time?
  Pre-planning (default taken for the first open question): The data is
  mostly there: planets and moons store `hill_radius_km`; each star
  stores `system_perimeter_km`, its Hill radius against the galaxy's
  tide (`spaceSector.hill_radius_ly`, already used to keep systems apart
  when they are placed); black holes, neutron stars and quasars have
  masses, so the same formula gives theirs. That answers the item's
  first open question: a star or lone object uses its galactic Hill
  radius.
  Research (2026-10-09, course-avoidance.md): inside a system a star's
  keep-out is its radiation radius `max(10 R_star, sqrt(L / (4 pi
  F_lim)))` with F_lim = 50 kW/m^2, and a neutron star or black hole
  inside a system uses its tide, field and radiation radius; the first
  open question is answered as already decided (galactic Hill radius for
  a lone star or object). Hops are bent one at a time; the route's stops
  do not change in practice (overhead 0.04% to 0.2% on average).

  Prerequisites: none.

    segment" in two parts: stars, neutron stars, rogue planets and small
    fields by the sectors the segment crosses plus a one-sector margin
    (their largest radius, 2.1 pc, is under one 4 pc sector edge); large
    kinds (intermediate black holes up to 25 pc, SMBH and quasar 2 to 10
    pc and up, nebulae up to 200 ly, remnants, large fields) by a
    bounding-box query on centre and radius, as
    `_placed_phenomenon_rows` does. Return `ref`, centre, radius, basis
    and note per object. An ungenerated sector has no objects to avoid;
    the answer says so (NAV.12's unknown-space flag already marks it).
    Scope after the review (2026-10-16 review): the obstacle query only;
    it returns each object's radius and basis from the keep-out table
    (NAV.54).
    Prerequisites: NAV.54.

  - [ ] **NAV.26 Bend the path around keep-out spheres**
    Done: a path planner that leaves the straight line only where it
    crosses a keep-out sphere, going around it on the shortest detour
    (a tangent arc, or waypoints just outside the sphere), checked
    again against the other spheres; the end bodies' own spheres are
    exempt (a ship has to enter them to arrive). Unit tests with
    hand-placed spheres.
    Asteroid fields count as keep-out areas too (Boss, 2026-10-09
    01:02Z: "Courses should avoid asteroid fields."), which NAV.51
    adds; nebulae and remnants stay pass-through with a note until Boss
    decides.
    Research (2026-10-09, course-avoidance.md): use the "insert wrap at
    first hit, then validated polish" method (section 5 of the design
    doc; the prototype needs only `math` and numpy). Exempt every sphere
    that contains an end, not only the end body's own. Add the overlap
    policy (cluster detection, enclosing sphere, flagged straight-line
    fallback `overlap_fallback`). Hand-placed tests: one sphere on the
    line (closed form), collinear start-centre-end, start inside a
    sphere, end on a surface, two spheres with a gap and with contact, a
    chain of wraps, 40 tiny spheres on a long line, an overlapping pair,
    a scene shifted by 2e4 pc (same answer). Say "short detour", not
    "shortest".
    Waits on NAV.62: the study of how the gravity of the stars a cell
    leaves out is added to the course (Boss, 2026-10-16, 5:01 PM EDT).
    Prerequisites: NAV.56, NAV.62, NAV.54.

  - [ ] **NAV.27 Moving bodies inside a system**
    Inside a system the planets move. Done: the in-system planner uses
    positions at the time of travel (MAP.62's positions-at-time module,
    Python twin), from the departure time and the leg's speed. That
    answers the item's second open question: yes. Default departure:
    now.
    Research (2026-10-09, course-avoidance.md): warp and fold speeds
    make departure-time positions sufficient, with the target aimed at
    its arrival-time position (`t0 + L/v`, 2 to 3 fixed-point steps);
    add the 3-to-6-pass iteration only if sub-0.01c speeds are
    introduced. `body_positions.positions_at` is the position source; no
    new ephemeris code. Galactic-scale motion is negligible at warp, so
    this stays system-only.
    Prerequisites: none.

- [ ] **NAV.54 One keep-out table for every kind of object: fields, supermassive holes and quasars, moons, stars in their own system, nebulae and remnants**
  NAV.24 shipped with these gaps: (a) asteroid fields get a hard
  keep-out of `radius_ly` in km, basis "radius" (NAV.51 asks for this;
  `galaxy/keepout.py` and `db/query.py` `keep_out_radius` return none
  today); (b) a supermassive hole or quasar keeps out a sphere of
  influence `G M / sigma^2` (sigma = 100 km/s, 1.7 pc at 4e6 solar
  masses), a quasar the larger of that and the 10 kW/m^2 radiation
  radius, not the event horizon (0.08 AU, which a course would graze);
  (c) a moon keeps out its Hill radius against the planet's mass; (d)
  the pass-through note for nebulae and remnants ("No mass is stored for

  remnants pass through with a
  note (chord length, column density, extinction) and no hard keep-out,
  with an optional soft cost later; a star inside its own system keeps
  out its radiation radius `max(10 R_star, sqrt(L / (4 pi F_lim)))`,
  F_lim = 50 kW/m^2 (0.17 AU for the Sun, 165 AU for an O3 star), hard
  and exempt when an end lies inside it; belts inside a system pass
  through with a note; the galactic centre keep-out of about 1.7 pc is
  exempt for any course to a star inside it.

- [ ] **GEN.40 Weed out sectors by star density before the bright-star backfill**
  Boss (2026-10-01 22:22Z): "see if we can cut down the number of
  sectors that need to be backfilled by taking the star density
  calculation and using it to weed out sectors from the star
  scattering. Might manage probability of getting a region through
  eliminating x number of sectors from the region so that the region
  probability matches what we're looking for. One pass would eliminate
  sectors based on probability, then the back fill would literally have
  less work to do. We would need to make sure that we don't over-filter
  though because bright stars in odd places is really neat and
  realistic." Today the GEN.30 backfill (`backfill_bright_stars_around`
  in `generate.py`, `brightStars.backfill_cells`) works out the
  densities and makes a Poisson draw for every unfilled sector of every
  block in range, most of which get no star. Investigate first; the
  subitems split the work.
  Research (2026-10-09, sampling-backfill-and-resume.md): fix the stale
  code pointers: the backfill is `generation/run_galaxy.py`
  `backfill_bright_stars_around` and `generation/bright_stars.py`
  `backfill_cells` (not `generate.py` and `brightStars`), drawn cell by
  cell in chunks of 200 sectors since GEN.44.

  - [ ] **GEN.42 A block-first draw for the backfill (umbrella)**
    One pass over a region (a sector block, or a tier's shell) uses the
    star density calculation (`galaxyDensity.population_densities`) to
    eliminate some of its sectors, chosen so that the region's chance of
    getting each bright star is still what the density says; the
    backfill then draws only in the sectors left. Done: the pass runs
    before the backfill, the backfill visits fewer sectors, and the same
    seed still gives the same stars wherever it lands (see GEN.39).
    Research (2026-10-09, sampling-backfill-and-resume.md): re-scope
    from "a pass that drops sectors" to an exact block-first draw for
    large volumes: a Poisson candidate count from the ring-and-layer
    density bound, then thinning, with the per-cell path kept for dense
    blocks (chosen per block: candidate path when expected candidates
    are under about 5% of the block's cells). The literal drop-and-boost
    form is rejected (dispersion 1.136 against 1.0, multiplicity
    chi-square 743,000 on 14 degrees of freedom). Done-test: the
    stratified multiplicity chi-square (half-decade strata of lambda,
    3,000+ replicates) run on the real `backfill_cells`, an assertion
    that every cell's rate is at most its block bound, and the order,
    partition and sub-region identity test. GEN.43's floor test becomes
    the lowest-lambda strata of this test (no cell's probability is
    altered, and `MIN_RELATIVE_DENSITY` keeps every cell above zero), so
    GEN.43 is folded in here. Answer to the GEN.41 question: no-go for
    the literal form; revisit when a run touches 10^5 or more cells. Ask
    PERF.31 to measure the SQL part at scale (2 ms per sector warm,
    about 0.8 ms of it SQL, plus a `sector_stats` row per visited
    sector). Include one block-first backfill in TEST.77's golden
    galaxy; the bound uses the `detmath` helpers.

- [ ] **GEN.105 Orbital updates**
  Boss (2026-10-03 and 2026-10-07) asked for an orbital update that
  moves only what has visibly moved, counts what changed, and lets
  nearby masses bend paths, with "reasonable limitations for when the
  math breaks down at the edge cases". `updateOrbits.py` is today's
  positional update. Time step, Boss (2026-10-07 17:11Z): "No 1 year
  per orbital update or turn, rather, once set up and configured we
  follow orbital paths in real time.  The update script should have an
  option to update for more time in 1 go if specified.  Default is 1
  day = 1 day." So each run advances the galaxy by the real time since
  its last update (one day of real time is one day of orbit), and an
  option advances it by a stated extra span in one go. Done when its
  subitems are.
  Boss statement (2026-10-18, 5:24 PM EDT): "And let's also double-check that the orbital motion updates:
  1. Checks for whatever records require an update. 2. New records
  without a next update field will always get an update, where the next
  update field will be set. 3. Calculate any required position changes
  first. 4. Change the motion vector of each object to account for
  gravitational effects, given the point mass, calculated gradient of
  the sector and area surrounding the sector, using the algorithm of:
  the largest hill radius present in the galaxy becomes the search
  radius for gravitational objects. So that we can calculate the vector
  field and the gravitational gradient at the exact location of the
  object to update its motion vector. Based on speed the system will
  then set an entry in the database for that object for when it next
  needs a position or motion update. According to the floor, it is
  already approved". The
  read-only check is [docs/design/orbits/orbital-update-check-2026-10-18.md](design/orbits/orbital-update-check-2026-10-18.md).
  The four steps are the order of one run: find the due records (a
  record with no next-update value is always due), advance each due
  object's position, change its motion vector from the influence set
  and the galactic gradient, then set its next-update value from its
  speed.
  Decided (Boss, card taps of 2026-10-18, 5:30 to 5:33 PM EDT, as the coordinator reported them (the cards are in the project chat; the tap results are not readable by this thread)). F1 search
  radius: the largest Hill radius of any object in the galaxy, one
  stored number, Sgr A* left out of that maximum (it is in the smooth
  potential); the nearest 64 are summed exactly and the rest as one
  point mass per sector; GEN.370 first so the radius uses the galaxy's
  own enclosed mass. F2: step 4 runs for every object through the one
  core function (amends card S13: a bound planet or moon works in its
  host's frame with the host's pull taken out; the tide screens stay as
  validity checks). F3 order: each object moves and then gets its vector in turn, not two phases (Boss's "position changes first" is read as position before vector within each object), in the chunk order set below (tier, then mass band), each chunk reading the state at its start, so the row order inside a chunk does not matter (reworded 2026-10-21, 7:45 AM EDT, to match the sweep answers on this item). F4 next due: the speed from the new vector,
  capped at the time for the influence set to change. F5 new records:
  always visited, the position advances only from the record's own
  epoch, then the next-update value is set. The last card, "Is the
  orbital motion update (your four steps) approved to build as
  written?", was answered "Approved as the cards say": the orbital
  motion update with F1 to F5 is APPROVED to build. That answers
  his unclear last sentence ("According to the floor, it is already
  approved"), whose meaning stays unknown. Where this note and older
  text on GEN.109, GEN.139, GEN.290, GEN.340, GEN.341, GEN.342 or
  orbital-updates.md differ, this note wins; those items are reworded
  as their lanes pick them up. Owner lane: Core 3, after its 8.1 queue,
  in the order GEN.370, GEN.341, GEN.342.
  Decided (Boss, 2026-10-18; his words 5:38 PM EDT, card tap "Tier first,
  then mass" as the coordinator reported it, 5:41 PM EDT): the order of
  the due objects is a stable sort on (tier, mass heaviest first, ties
  by id). Boss: "Overall this should support our most massive to least
  massive. Even within the galactic span high-mass objects are moved
  before low-mass objects. Objects in the galactic frame of reference
  ... such as a rogue planet, an interstellar comet, or a single primary
  star, should all be moved before anything inside a system." Tier is
  the number of hops from the galactic frame, derived from the parent
  link and not stored; the names are labels only: tier 0 (his
  "primary") is every top-level object (rogues, interstellar comets,
  single stars, each system's primary), tier 1 ("secondary") is planets
  and companion stars, tier 2 ("tertiary") is moons, tier 3 ("quinary")
  is small moon satellites; a rogue planet's moon is tier 1. Rows run in
  ordered chunks (tier, then mass band), each seeing the state at its
  start. A planet heavier than a companion star stays in its tier and is
  ordered by mass there (the "bizarre quirk" he accepts); a capture in
  the middle of a run takes effect in the next run's order. Open
  measurement: the sort cost on millions of due rows is not measured yet.
  Headline: 8.3 (the orbital update system).
  Prerequisites: GEN.290, GEN.291.
  Design: [docs/design/orbits/orbital-updates.md](design/orbits/orbital-updates.md)
  Research (2026-10-09, orbital-solvers-and-integrators.md): the Full
  Algorithm's one-year macro step and "nightly" language are superseded
  by real time: perturbation integration is per due object over its
  whole interval with an adaptive integrator (`DOP853`; IAS15-class for
  encounters), not Velocity Verlet in day steps. REBOUND is not a
  dependency (GPL-3.0-only against CC0). The text "`updateOrbits.py` is
  today's positional update" is stale: the code is `planetgen orbits`

  Update (2026-10-09, after Boss supplied the paper): the implementable
  Vynatheya et al. 2022 form (MNRAS 516, 4146; arXiv 2207.03151v2) is
  its Equation 4: q_out = m3 / (m1 + m2); e_in,max = sqrt(1 - 5/3 cos^2
  i); e_in,avg = 0.5 e_in,max^2; the effective inner eccentricity is
  max(e_in, e_in,avg), and equals e_in where cos^2 i > 3/5 (our choice;
  the paper is silent); Y = a_out (1 - e_out) / [a_in (1 + e_in_eff)];
  Y_crit = 2.4 [(1 + q_out) / ((1 + e_in_eff) (1 - e_out)^(1/2))]^(2/5)
  x [((1 - 0.2 e_in_eff + e_out) / 8) (cos i - 1) + 1]; stable if Y >
  Y_crit. It was fitted for 0.01 <= q_in <= 1, 0.01 <= q_out <= 100 and
  1e-4 < alpha < 1. Accuracy against N-body runs (paper Table 4): EK95
  0.86, MA01 0.90, Equation 4 0.93, the paper's neural net 0.95 (its
  weights were not reachable, so it is not implementable). Decided by

- [ ] **GEN.198 The gravity field evaluator: pull, potential and tidal gradient at any point from the point masses and the galaxy potential**
  Boss (2026-10-10 20:57Z): the orbits come from point-mass vectors, so
  the same masses give a gravitational field. Done: one function
  returns, for any point and time, the acceleration vector, the
  potential and the tidal tensor (its largest eigenvalue and the size of
  the gradient) from the point masses in and around a sector (the
  influence set of GEN.109) plus the galaxy's smooth potential
  (GEN.115), with Plummer softening; near sources are summed exactly and
  distant ones as per-region aggregates (PERF.72 sets the split). It is
  a pure function of the stored vectors, so the same galaxy gives the
  same field, and course planning (NAV.6) does not use it: it plans
  around keep-out spheres.
  Note (2026-10-10): Boss (22:14Z) asked that the size of each gradient
  measure be built from the preset minimum movement values of the
  orbital update system (THRESHOLDS_M in physics/position.py: galactic
  0.01 mpc, about 2 AU; system 0.01 AU; planetary 100,000 km). The
  gradient step of the evaluator is the threshold of the scale being
  drawn (galactic for a sector, system for the System Map, planetary for
  a moon neighbourhood), read from the same constants, not a copy. See
  the new section in docs/design/orbits/gravity-map.md.
  Prerequisites: GEN.342. Related: GEN.105, NAV.6, PERF.72,
  MAP.167.
  Scope after the review (2026-10-16 review): the tidal tensor and its
  eigenvalue, the galaxy potential term (GEN.115, GEN.285), the near and
  far split with per-region aggregates and the gradient step from
  THRESHOLDS_M; pull and potential at a point come from the field kernel
  (PERF.88). Course planning (NAV.6) reuses nothing from it: NAV.6,
  NAV.25 and NAV.26 plan around keep-out spheres.
  Consolidation sweep (Boss, 2026-10-16, 11:58 PM EDT; applied
  2026-10-17): TEST.131 folded in. Its tests are part of this item and
  land in the same PR (Test Suite Rebuild decision, 2026-10-14): the
  evaluator matches Newton for two bodies to 1e-9 relative; the
  Sun-Earth L1 and L2 points land near 1.5 million km with a saddle in
  the tidal gradient; it stays finite inside a softened source; the
  galaxy potential's rotation curve matches the published one (a
  plausibility target only); the near and far split agrees with the
  exact sum to a stated tolerance on a random sector; the same seed
  gives the same field twice.

- [ ] **GEN.199 Per-zone gravity grid for a sector: stored in a cache and rebuilt when the orbits update**
  Done: for a sector, the field (GEN.198) is sampled at the centre of
  each zone (16 per edge by default, a setting), giving the pull, the
  potential and the tidal strength per zone, with Lagrange and saddle
  points flagged. The grid is derived data held in a cache like the
  Galaxy Map tiles (not in the galaxy tables, so no galaxy migration),
  is built on the work queue, is thrown away when the orbital update
  (GEN.105) moves its sources, and a sector with no neighbours generated
  yet is marked uncharted-edge. A test builds a small sector and checks
  the grid against the evaluator zone by zone.
  Note (2026-10-10): Boss (22:14Z) asked that the size of each gradient
  measure be built from the preset minimum movement values of the
  orbital update system (THRESHOLDS_M in physics/position.py: galactic
  0.01 mpc, about 2 AU; system 0.01 AU; planetary 100,000 km). A zone
  edge is a whole number of those steps (the default sector zone of 0.25
  pc is 25,000 galactic steps) and never finer than one step; a cached
  zone is thrown away only when a source passes its own threshold, the
  same event that sets its next update due time (GEN.106). PERF.72 sets
  the multiples.
  Prerequisites: GEN.198, PERF.72. Related: GEN.105, PERF.72, MAP.167.

  a NumPy batch takes 3.8 us and refiles the same addresses on 100,000

- [ ] **GEN.290 An encounter search that cannot miss a pass at large steps (100 years per second)**
  Finding (orbital-encounters research, 2026-10-15, kind: gap in
  GEN.109): GEN.109 describes forces from nearby bodies but no search
  for close passes that stays safe when one step covers many years. A
  pass at speed v and distance b needs a slice well under b / v (a
  star-on-star pass at 40 km/s and 1,000 AU takes about 120 years), so a
  century in one step steps straight over it. Done: a design for
  stepping each object in slices short enough that a pass is never
  missed, or an analytic closest-approach test between the paths of
  nearby bodies over the whole step (a body with a mass at or above the
  host's, such as a black hole or a neutron star, first), so that a
  system is switched to the sub-stepped integrator only while a
  perturber is inside its Hill sphere or its planets' orbits and every
  other system keeps the cheap clockwork; the cost estimate on the
  benchmark galaxy; and a test with a seeded black hole passing a seeded
  system at a large step. Source: Boss's question of 2026-10-15 at 10:53
  PM EDT (if the orbital motion ran 100 years of movement in 1 second,
  what would the program account for when a black hole or neutron star
  got close to a planetary system, and would planets be ejected?) and
  its answer, /mnt/project-files/research/orbital-encounters/answer.md.
  Boss asked on 2026-10-15 (11:06 PM EDT) for these gaps to be filled;
  they join the Phase 2 and 3 workflow and no lane builds them yet.
  Placement: Phase 2, after GEN.109 and GEN.289. Passing bodies (black
  holes, neutron stars, any body at or above the host's mass) are
  searched first; GEN.109's Hill-sphere influence radius decides who
  joins a system's set. Boss's design (2026-10-15, 11:06 PM EDT): at
  each step in which orbital changes are calculated, a planet or moon is
  moved by the summed gravitational influence of point masses (the
  vector of the gravitational gradient of the space it occupies), the
  other planets and moons of its system counted by their point masses
  too, plus passing objects such as black holes and neutron stars, so
  planets can be captured or ejected; the orbital path comes out right
  and agrees with the pass-through-the-sphere logic (the sector-crossing
  guard of GEN.223 and GEN.265).
  Prerequisites: GEN.343. Related: GEN.105,
  GEN.109,
  GEN.110,
  GEN.115,
  GEN.223.
  Scope after the review (2026-10-16 review): deciding per system when
  to switch to the perturbed pass (passing bodies of host mass or more
  first, the system-radius filter from the first child of GEN.109), the
  cost estimate on the benchmark galaxy and the seeded black-hole test;
  the closest-approach maths comes from the library.
  Reworded to match GEN.105 (contradiction sweep, 2026-10-21, 7:45 AM
  EDT; GEN.105's Decided notes win where this item's older text
  differs): the encounter search runs inside the same visit order (tier,
  then mass band, chunk-start state) and uses the one global search
  radius (largest Hill radius, GEN.370 first) to decide who joins a
  system's set; a bound planet or moon works in its host's frame with
  the host's pull taken out (F2).

- [ ] **GEN.295 Nebulae as point groups whose shape follows the orbital update (design and research)**
  Boss asked (2026-10-16, 1:01 AM EDT, project chat): "should nebulae be
  a group of points that then as orbits update the nebula changes
  shape?" Answer given to him: yes in principle, it follows from GEN.294
  (every object one SpatialPosition3D with point mass and movement
  vector). Design and research only, nothing built, no lane. Today a
  nebula is one point (centre, one scalar galactic_orbital_speed_kms,
  epoch_unix, radius_ly as a bounding sphere) plus a shape fixed when it
  was made: 4 to 8 metaballs in nebula_shape_balls (centre and radius,
  no mass, no velocity) and the ellipsoid, warp, noise and isovalue
  columns (GEN.75, galaxy/nebula_shape.py); it moves rigidly and never
  changes shape. Done: a design note
  (docs/design/nebulae-as-point-groups.md, with its
  docs/design/README.md row) that answers: (1) the points: each a
  SpatialPosition3D with mass and vector (cloud parcels), how many per
  nebula by class (the 4 to 8 balls today, or tens for fidelity), and
  the storage cost per count (seven doubles and a key is about 80 bytes
  a point, so 8 points over the 163,000 field clouds of classes M and N
  is about 100 MB [C], to be checked against
  nebula-density-vs-reality.md); whether the small P and Q clouds stay
  single points; (2) how the shape and bounds are derived at each
  update: the metaball field summed from the points' masses and radii,
  the isovalue, the bounding radius_ly and the containment tests
  (inside_nebula_id, the stars placed inside by GEN.241, the map's soft
  sprites MAP.176/MAP.178) recomputed, and when a stored shape is
  rebuilt rather than carried; (3) what point-mass gravity cannot
  capture and what stands in for it: gas pressure and turbulence,
  magnetic fields, radiation pressure and photoionisation, shocks, star
  formation consuming the gas, stellar feedback, and the expansion of
  supernova remnants and planetary nebulae (analytic radius against age
  rather than gravity); (4) the timescale: a giant molecular cloud of 30
  pc crossing at about 3 km/s takes about 10 Myr [C], galactic shear
  (Oort A about 15 km/s/kpc) shapes a cloud over a few tens of Myr [C],
  so shape change is invisible at one day a step and shows only on long
  steps (GEN.292) such as 1 Myr, about three hours at 100 years a
  second; (5) a recommendation, including whether the points orbit under
  GEN.109's influence rule or only the galaxy's potential (GEN.115) and
  a cap per nebula so the nightly cost stays bounded (PERF.103's row ceiling counts every point). Source:
  Boss's question and the coordinator's answer. Phase 3, after GEN.294,
  GEN.109 and GEN.292.
  Prerequisites: GEN.292. Related: GEN.75, GEN.115,
  GEN.241, GEN.289, GEN.293, MAP.176, MAP.178.

- [ ] **GEN.297 Calibrate the cluster generator against the Harris file: its distributions guide the laws, and no real cluster is placed in any galaxy**
  Boss (2026-10-16, 4:11 PM EDT, in the TODO thread): "There should be
  no option to pick a Milky Way preset. The Harris file is designed to
  give you an idea of how to build the procedure to generate a realistic
  galaxy." Follow-up from Core 2 (2026-10-16, 7:52 AM EDT, GEN.159
  merged as #1810, migration 0097): the cluster table
  (galaxy_components), the King tables and solver and a seeded generator
  are built. Done: the Harris file (kept at
  /mnt/project-files/data/harris/mwgc.dat) is read by a reference reader
  used by the tests and the design note, never loaded into a galaxy; the
  generator's laws (the count from the halo mass, the mass
  function, the radial profiles of the halo and bulge groups, the
  bimodal [Fe/H], the King concentration, the age spread) are calculated
  or derived from published science and checked against the file's
  distributions statistically, not row for row; a test shows the
  generated population matches the file's medians and spreads within
  stated bounds; the design note records the file's version, licence and
  the mass-to-light assumption. There is no Milky Way option and no real
  cluster (47 Tuc, Omega Centauri, M13) appears by name. Owner: Core 3,
  in the cluster line. The file arrived 2026-10-16, 3:04 PM EDT. The
  file: Harris 1996 (2010 edition), December 2010 revision, 157 clusters
  in three parts. Part I has the name, RA and Dec, galactic longitude
  and latitude, the distance from the Sun and from the Galactic centre
  (R0 = 8.0 kpc) and X, Y, Z; Part II the [Fe/H], reddening, V magnitude
  of the horizontal branch, distance modulus, integrated V, M_V, the
  colours, spectral type and ellipticity; Part III the radial velocity,
  dispersion, King concentration c (a "c" marks a core-collapsed
  cluster), core and half-light radii in arcminutes, central surface
  brightness and luminosity density, and the relaxation times. It has no
  mass and no age: the reader takes mass from M_V with a stated
  mass-to-light ratio and says so; gaps in a column fall back to the
  generator's own laws. Licence: free to use if the original source is
  named; cite "Harris 1996 (2010 edition)" in the design note and the
  file header. GEN.237 merged (#1851, 2026-10-16, 3:15 PM EDT): the
  component table exists.

- [ ] **GEN.371 Feasibility study: generate the satellite galaxies through the scatter, making only the region each one occupies**
  Boss (2026-10-16, 4:02 PM EDT, in the Core 1 thread): "we'll need a
  feasibility study. I would like to generate them in the scatter if
  possible, even if we just generate the region that they are in." Done:
  a written study (a section beside 5.5 of
  docs/design/galaxy/intergalactic-and-halo-contents.md) that answers whether a
  drawn satellite can be made by the same scatters as the rest of the
  sphere, so its stars, gas and clusters come from the one rule set and
  a profile, and what it costs when only the cells the satellite
  occupies are generated. It covers the profile a satellite cell needs
  (its density law, [Fe/H], age and star-formation history), how the
  cell key and the 96-bit ID address a satellite's cells, how many cells
  and systems a dwarf, the Clouds and a Sagittarius-sized stream make at
  the default cell size, the run time per satellite by the measured cost
  per cell, how the component pass GEN.324 and the cluster chain feed
  it, and a recommendation with the work it needs as new items. No build
  in this item. Owner: Core 1, with GEN.368, after the global top 5
  blockers unless Boss moves it up.
  Boss (2026-10-16, 4:04 PM EDT, in the Core 1 thread): "we don't need
  them to be the exact distances. What we need is for that to be
  calculated or derived or generated, preferably calculated and derived
  using real science." The study also reports which of a satellite's
  properties can be calculated rather than drawn from the halo mass and
  the galaxy's history, and what the scatter needs to make its region
  from those.
  The study follows the same chain: the galaxy's halo mass from its own
  mass model -> virial radius -> subhalo count from the subhalo mass
  function (dN/dM roughly M^-1.9, from the Aquarius and Via Lactea
  simulations) -> radial placement from a subhalo profile (less
  concentrated than the dark matter) -> stellar mass from the
  stellar-to-halo mass relation (abundance matching) with a low-mass
  cutoff for reionization -> size from the size-mass relation -> [Fe/H]
  from the mass-metallicity relation (Kirby 2013) -> age and profile
  from the mass and gas fraction, with tidal stripping near the disk.
  Each link names its source in the doc and the code. The real Milky Way
  rows serve only as a check that the derived population looks
  plausible.
  Boss (2026-10-16, 4:14 PM EDT, in the TODO thread): "I want to
  reiterate that the idea is that we generate a scientifically accurate
  galaxy as best we can. We generate the sectors of that, again as
  accurately as we can, with what we can actually do processing-wise and
  what we actually know. Astrophysics-wise that can be implemented I
  don't want any fixed content. Everything should be procedurally
  generated based on the random seeds that we already use. Random
  numbers are used where we can. Things are derived everywhere we can or
  calculated everywhere we can. If needed you should ask me to do
  research if there are pieces missing that you can't look up yourself."
  Decided (Boss, 2026-10-16, 9:16 PM EDT, card "Both next"; relayed by
  the coordinator): Core 1 does it right after GEN.369 (order: GEN.368,
  GEN.369, GEN.371, GEN.366). Owner: Core 1.
  Decided (Boss, contradiction sweep cards, taps 6:10 to 6:12 PM EDT
  2026-10-18, as the coordinator reported them): fork 13: GEN.369 no
  longer waits on this study.
  Prerequisites: none. Related: GEN.368, GEN.369, GEN.324, GEN.237.
  Design: [docs/design/galaxy/intergalactic-and-halo-contents.md](design/galaxy/intergalactic-and-halo-contents.md)

- [ ] **GEN.477 The asteroid belt and field composition is drawn from the star, the distance and the belt's mass, not four names drawn uniformly from a list of 84 (bug)**
  Finding F11 of the Body composition research lane (section 14.5 of
  docs/design/composition/body-composition-research.md, tables E1 to E4; 2026-10-17,
  1:47 AM EDT as the lane reported, read from the code at the commit it
  names), filed by the TODO thread. `generate_asteroid_composition`
  (src/planetgen/generation/belt.py 29-60, called from
  `AsteroidBelt.__init__`) takes four components by
  `draw.sample(ASTEROID_COMPONENTS, k=4)` from a flat list of 84 names
  (tuning.py 196-215: 16 elements including gold and the platinum-group
  metals, 13 rock-forming and metal minerals, 8 rare-earth, 6
  platinum-group, 7 uranium and thorium, 7 titanium species, 14 oxides,
  salts, carbonates and gem minerals, 4 garnets, 2 micas, chrysoberyl
  and six polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons), shuffles them and gives
  them the levels high, moderate, small and trace, so gold or coronene
  is as likely to be the high component as olivine. The draw does not
  read the star, the belt's distance, the snow line, the [Fe/H] or the
  belt's mass; the belt density (dense, sparse, typical) is a separate
  uniform draw (belt.py 138); only four words are stored
  (`asteroid_belt_composition`, db/models.py 20-34). Standalone asteroid
  fields (generation/phenomena/asteroid_field.py) draw one of eight
  families by frequencies (carbonaceous 30, stony 20, icy 20, mixed 10,
  metallic 8, dust 5, basaltic 4, collisional 3) that carry no source,
  then 5 to 9 components uniformly from a per-family list (`mixed` and
  `collisional` sample the same 84 names). Do, in the gated format of
  GEN.472: (E1) gate the belt components by object kind and draw the
  belt's taxon mixture from the taxon table of GEN.457 and GEN.442 (the
  zone kernel in a / a_snow of the system's own snow line, GEN.458; a
  flagged `stand-in` until GEN.473 replaces it), with the components
  following from the taxon's analogue chemistry, the 84-name list kept
  only as a vocabulary of names; (E2) the belt density follows the
  belt's mass per area from the disc and not a separate draw; (E3) the
  eight field families are a gated possibility table whose frequencies
  are flagged `stand-in` (no source), replaced under GEN.473 by the
  composition of the system whose bodies the field was stripped from, or
  by a derived population; (E4) each family's component list comes from
  the analogue chemistry of its taxon, the family names kept as labels.
  Stored data (part D 3.6 keeps `composition_summary` as derived text):
  a belt stores its taxon mass shares and the mass fractions of its main
  components (iron, nickel, olivine, pyroxene, phyllosilicates, water,
  carbon, metal; the columns are DB.70), and the four-level words come
  from those fractions by fixed thresholds (for example above 20 percent
  of the belt mass high, 5 to 20 moderate, 1 to 5 small, below 1 trace)
  and not from a draw; exotic minerals (rare-earth, platinum-group,
  radioactive, gem, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons) become accessory
  species included only when the chemistry supports them (a ppm

  behind its queue).
  Prerequisites: none. Related: GEN.528, GEN.526, GEN.319.

- [ ] **GEN.537 Design the plan configuration: the boundaries of the sector plan, how far scatters go, which sector addresses are valid, and the two switches halo and satellite galaxies (both default off)**
  Boss, 2026-10-17, 4:31 PM EDT: "begin planning for the halo and
  intergalactic generation to be a switch that defaults to off, put that
  in for 8.5 please, we'll get it working first." Changed by Boss,
  2026-10-17, 4:48 PM EDT: "Make there be 2 switches, halo and satellite
  galaxies, both default to off, halo doesn't mean satellite galaxies,
  they are separate commands used to configure the plan. That plan
  configuration tells scatter and sector generation the boundaries of
  the sector plan and control how far scatters can go around the galaxy
  and what sector addresses are valid." What exists (read from main,
  2026-10-17): the plan's boundaries are `GalaxyBounds`
  (galaxy/skeleton.py): the reach (`reach_shell_index`, set by `plan
  --reach-shells`, stored in `galaxy_shape` with the outline in
  `galaxy_shell`), whose `contains` says which sector addresses are
  valid and is today the only refusal a generation path has (GEN.235),
  and the outline, whose `qualifies` is where the paths that pick cells
  nobody named stay; how far a scatter goes is not in the plan but the
  program constant `tuning.SCATTER_COVERS_REACH = True`, read in
  generation/run_plan.py (the bright-star and phenomena scatters);
  satellite galaxies are placed unconditionally by
  `satellites.place_satellites` inside the plan build (run_plan.py,
  `generation/satellites.py`). Version 8.1 builds the halo and the
  satellite galaxies first, always on (GEN.301). Done: a design note
  (docs/design) that settles, with Boss by card: (1) the plan
  configuration as the single source of the boundaries of the sector
  plan, how far each scatter can go around the galaxy, and which sector
  addresses are valid, read by the scatter commands and by sector
  generation, which never decide those themselves (it replaces the
  `SCATTER_COVERS_REACH` constant and the reach and outline checks
  scattered through generation, and extends `GalaxyBounds`, which
  already holds the reach and the outline); (2) two switches, halo and
  satellite galaxies, both default off and independent (halo does not
  mean satellite galaxies): what each adds to the valid addresses and to
  the scatter reach (halo: the cells beyond the outline out to the reach
  and the scatter rows there; satellite galaxies: the volumes of the
  satellite galaxies and their stars, which may lie beyond the outline),
  and what off means (nothing generated or stored there, the interior
  the same stars for the same seed whether either is on or off, an
  address outside the configured boundaries answers "outside the
  generated galaxy" with the reason); (3) each switch is set by its own
  command under the one-command rule (PERF.118, PERF.120): a halo
  command and a satellite-galaxies command, each doing only that and
  writing only the plan configuration, with their own parameters; the
  262 kpc reach and the 96-bit IDs stay as addressing; (4) where the
  configuration is stored (proposed: beside the galaxy shape, set by a
  migration from what an existing galaxy holds, so a galaxy built in 8.1
  with both on keeps them on, and default off for a galaxy created after
  8.5); (5) what turning a switch on later does (the missing part only,
  no interior regeneration) and what turning it off does (generation
  stops and the maps hide it; deleting what exists is the separate admin
  delete); (6) how the wrapper uses it: the step list holds the halo and
  satellite commands only when the configuration allows them, so a
  switch that is off means those commands are never selected and never
  touched. Owner: the design thread (coordinator to assign); Boss
  approves the choices by card.
  Prerequisites: none. Related: GEN.301, PERF.118, PERF.121, GEN.235,
  MAP.243, MAP.207.
  Added (Boss, 2026-10-17, 4:49 PM EDT: "the galaxy setting will also
  tell the scatter functions if they can scatter the halo and / or the
  satellite galaxies, either / or"): the stored galaxy setting (halo on
  or off, satellite galaxies on or off) is read by every scatter
  command, and each scatter kind checks only the switch that concerns
  it: the halo scatter kinds read the halo switch, the satellite and
  satellite-component scatter kinds read the satellite switch, the kinds
  that concern neither (the disc, bulge and core scatters) read neither;
  either switch can be on without the other. The design settles which
  scatter kind reads which switch.
  Decided (Boss, 2026-10-17, card tapped 4:56 PM EDT, "Migrate in 8.5",
  relayed by the coordinator): a galaxy created in 8.1 keeps its halo
  and satellite content, and the 8.5 migration sets that galaxy's halo
  and satellite galaxy switches to on if it holds that content (each
  switch on its own); only a galaxy created after 8.5 defaults both off.
  No change to 8.1. Point (4) of this design is therefore settled.
  Decided (Boss, 9:02 PM EDT 2026-10-21, tapped "Answer now", card
  cmsg_01RuNTFUNB92A8cm5CbojQAiQEpSHqXuHrfwkEi57MUfJd): the plan
  configuration cards are answered now, not at 8.5. A design thread
  posts the cards (boundaries, scatter reach, the halo and satellite
  switches, storage) and writes docs/design from the answers; the
  coordinator starts it. 8.1 still builds halo and satellites always on
  (GEN.301).
  Decided (Boss, 2026-10-21, 9:21 to 9:24 PM EDT, eight cards in the
  Plan configuration design thread; report
  /mnt/project-files/reports/gen537-plan-configuration-decisions-2026-10-22.md):
  (1) Boundaries: the 262 kpc addressing ceiling (`reach_shell_index`,
  96-bit IDs) stays stored, with a halo reach and a satellite reach
  added below it; the outline stays derived by `plan` (the Edge dial,
  GEN.605); valid addresses are the outline, plus the halo region out to
  the halo reach when halo is on, plus the satellite volumes when
  satellite galaxies are on. (2) An address beyond the switches is
  refused with the reason ("outside the generated galaxy", naming the
  switch that is off); this supersedes the GEN.235 rule that any address
  inside the reach is generated on demand and the `outside_ok` path
  (GEN.81); 8.9 "generate anywhere" may reopen it. (3) The halo reach
  defaults to the 262 kpc ceiling; the halo command takes a smaller
  reach in L, pc, kpc or Mpc like the Edge dial and shows the expected
  rows and time first; no virial-radius default (its ratio has no
  source). (4) By place: beyond the outline everything that is not a
  satellite galaxy follows the halo switch (stellar halo, halo globular
  clusters, hypervelocity and ejected stars, high-velocity clouds, hot
  halo gas); satellite galaxies and their own stars, clusters and
  phenomena follow the satellite switch; anything inside the outline is
  always generated. (5) `scatter` keeps one kind per run and gains one
  region parameter (interior, halo or satellites); the wrapper's step
  list holds one run per kind per region the configuration enables;
  completion is stored per kind and region, so turning a switch on later
  runs only the missing regions; this replaces the 4:49 PM EDT
  2026-10-17 wording that each scatter kind reads only its switch. (6)
  The satellite switch is on or off only; count, places and sizes always
  come from the seed's draw (GEN.369); same seed, same satellites; no
  distance cap and no count dial for now. (7) Switching off keeps stored
  content visible (not the recommended option): only generation stops;
  stored rows stay drawn, searchable and routable. (8) Storage: a new
  one-row `plan_configuration` table holding the two switches, the halo
  reach, the satellite reach and the ceiling (moved out of
  `galaxy_shape`); only the halo and satellite commands write it; `plan`
  reads it and never rewrites it; it joins the plan fingerprint tables
  (`PLAN_TABLES` in `db/fingerprint.py`); the 8.5 migration fills it
  from what an existing galaxy holds. Applied defaults, not carded: if a
  new `plan` outline would grow past a stored halo reach, `plan` refuses
  and names the halo command; a request to generate beyond the
  boundaries is refused but a sector with stored content stays readable
  for display, search and routing after its switch is turned off; the
  halo and satellite commands refuse a galaxy that has nothing to switch
  on (below the halo threshold `dials.HALO_MIN_HALO_MASS_SOLAR`,
  GEN.606; a satellite draw of none, GEN.369), saying why; turning a
  switch on later makes only the missing region. The design note in
  docs/design is written from the report; confirm with the design
  thread.
  Pending detail (Boss, 2026-10-21, 9:26 PM EDT, a sub-option to the
  switch decision, "admin should have the ability to switch off halo's
  to a made galaxy but it would be destructive and actually remove them
  from the database and make all halo cells invalid addresses"): besides
  the non-destructive switch-off (card 7, stored content stays), an
  admin can switch the halo off on an already-made galaxy destructively:
  the halo content is removed from the database and every halo cell
  becomes an invalid address (refused with the reason, decision 2). The
  Plan configuration design thread is working out the specifics
  (confirmation, what exactly is deleted, the fingerprint and the
  completion records, whether satellites get the same) and reports;
  until then it is a pending detail, not a decision.

  host: draw its companion nodes when its table has them and depth
  allows, draw the orbiters of every satellite row that passes the gate
  inside the zone rule (engulfment and Roche limit to the Holman-Wiegert
  limit for a binary or the Hill sphere in the galaxy for a single star;
  for a planet, the Roche limit to 0.4895 of the Hill radius, prograde),

  built from `Stream(f"{host_seed}:orbit:{slot}")`, so building a system

  host logic of `StarSystem._generate_planets`, `generate_moons` and the
  stage C system pass (`SYSTEM_PASS_ODDS`). The fill keeps its stage
  letters and one random stream per stage (GEN.251), so no other stage's
  draw moves. A star system is then the recursion: group, member,
  planet, moon. Done: a system rebuilt from its stored members and seeds

  is not measured: -2.5 (collisional cascade), -3 (broad), -3.8
  (free-floating planets), and steeper than -3 is needed so mass does
  not diverge; draw the cumulative index over 2.5 to 3.8 per galaxy as a
  labelled stand-in (widest range rule). (3) Keep the remnant-mass-cut
  device: choose a lowest size by how many rows a sector may hold (with
  index 3 there are 8.8e14 per pc^3 above 100 m and about 1 above 10^4
  km). (4) Bound long-period comets (Oort cloud, Boe et al. 2019:
  cumulative index about 3.6 above 1 km, nearly flat from 100 m to 1 km)
  are a different population from the unbound ones this item covers. (5)
  Dryness: the cometary fraction must be below 2.4e-4 per au^3, so dry
  objects like Oumuamua need a rocky share above 0.9988 if the comet
  density is the limit. Not read: the body of Boe 2019 and the Fig. 19

  `PlanetaryObject` (`Planet` with its `is_moon`, `RoguePlanet`: a moon

  field members). Rule: subclass only where behaviour differs and the
  object never changes kind; anything that can change or is a matter of
  degree is state or parent data. Groups (the nodes of a multi-star

  about 34 orders of magnitude of mass (1.05e6 kg for a 10 m rock to the
  2.0e40 kg black hole), with every position relative to the parent,
  never galaxy-absolute (10 m at 262 kpc is a relative precision of
  1e-21, beyond a double); rows are generated from each population's own
  cut (a planet or moon always, a comet above its size cut, belt members
  on demand: the k-th largest member of a belt is a pure function of the
  belt's seed and k, nothing stored). E4: the core is planned to take

  formed from relative numbers only (a double at 8 kpc has a spacing of

  in any ancestor's frame is the sum of the hops, leaf first, each hop
  advanced from its own epoch (analytic two-body orbit with mu = G
  (M_central + M_member); the outer system's tide is a stability gate,
  not a force). The step that makes the heaviest primary is GEN.581.

  analytic two-body orbit per frame with mu including the member's own

  frames or any other point, found through the lowest common ancestor;
  S15 a point has a live parent link with a versioned cache and the
  copied anchors and the three `carry_*` calls go; S16 the point holds a
  kinematic record (position, velocity, spin axis and rate, mass with
  mu, epoch and next-due) with identity, radius and age beside it in the
  core; S17 spin is a unit axis plus an angular rate in rad/s; S18
  speed, axial tilt, galactic orbital period and phase, rotation period
  and a* become derived and their columns are dropped in the 8.4
  revision with DB.73). Boss's refinements of 12:23, 12:24 and 12:25 AM
  EDT, 2026-10-18 (project chat, as the coordinator relayed): any two
  objects that orbit each other follow one rule; before a system is
  validated the heaviest object becomes the primary and the others are
  recalculated from their original values; the barycentre is always the
  origin; coordinates are relative at every level, so a moon follows its
  planet and the planet follows the star; the point-in-space object
  updates the relative coordinates, knows its centre's position in wider
  space and gives converted coordinates for any frame on demand; and it
  also stores the vector of motion, the spin and the other attributes of
  the object with a mass classification. Item SY12 of the note (sections
  10.2 to 10.6). Proposed owner, not assigned by a card: Core 3 for the
  function and the pair builder (GEN.555) with Core 4 for `populate`
  (GEN.556). Do: one function `primary_first(members)` in the host
  chain: collect the members with their original values, rank them by
  total branch mass (a sub-system counts as the sum of its parts; a tie
  under 1e-9 relative keeps the draw order, so the step is stable and
  idempotent and does not depend on the order members are listed), nest
  by distance (members inside the demoted body's stable zone stay with
  it as a sub-system, members outside the pair's orbit orbit the pair's
  barycentre, members in the unstable gap are moved or dropped by the
  existing outermost-first rule), recompute everything that depends on
  the primary from the original values, then validate. Two bodies:
  re-primarying a pair is a relabel plus a sign (the relative position
  is negated, the phase moves by 180 degrees, the elements and the
  barycentre are unchanged) and every absolute position is identical.
  The four copies of the swap retire to it: `multistar._Builder.place`
  (line 620), `generation/system.py:299-308`,
  `generation/wide_binary.py:119-121` and `generation/binary.py`
  (GEN.316 already retires the two-star classes). GEN.555 and GEN.556
  need it. Done: a pair re-primaried gives identical absolute positions,
  the step from the originals is idempotent and independent of listing
  order, and no second copy of the swap is left.
  Prerequisites: GEN.315. Related: GEN.550, GEN.565, GEN.576, GEN.578.
  Design: [docs/design/architecture/unified-system-barycentre.md](design/architecture/unified-system-barycentre.md)

- [ ] **GEN.648 The generation request for a habitable world (+habitable_world) runs an ordered ladder of nine adaptations before it gives up: redraw the surface, restrict the planet, more starting water, aquifers, regenerate the planet, adapt the system, add a brighter primary, regenerate the star, then the best result**
  Decided (Boss, 6:09 PM EDT 2026-10-23, card option 3 of GEN.644, 'A
  then D', relayed by the coordinator): 'Let's go with 3, since we're
  doing compositions, let's leave out the class designation until planet
  generation is completed, then fill in the classes based on the
  atmosphere (even no atmosphere) composition / pressure, average
  surface temperature, terrestrial composition (i.e. a rocky planet
  composition), gas composition (for gas giants), same for moons. The
  reason I did classes the way they are now is because I didn't know how
  to get the compositions correct.' Proposal and options:
  /mnt/project-files/reports/phi6-and-planet-classes-proposal-2026-10-23.md
  (options A, B, C are retired). Part of GEN.644 (design) and GEN.643
  (the habitable rule). Owner: Habitability lane D unless stated.
  Replace the class-list steering (LIFE_PLANET_CLASSES). Boss (7:12 PM
  EDT 2026-10-23, answering through lane D): a habitable-world request
  runs an ordered ladder of adaptations before it quits. After each
  attempt the failing domain of the finished score (Water, Temperature,
  Radiation, Suitability) and the star's history loss pick the next step.
  The aim is a PHI-6 overall of Blue or Green; the accepted end is Yellow
  with Suitability at least Yellow (Boss, 6:54 PM EDT). The ladder:
  (1) redraw the surface (albedo, greenhouse, atmosphere, life draws of
  the same planet); (2) restrict the planet parameters (mass 0.5 to 2
  Earth masses, rocky, low eccentricity, usable rotation and tilt);
  (3) more starting water, an Ocean World (initial water = the history
  loss / mass plus an Earth-like remainder; the class follows the
  finished composition under GEN.644 option 3); (4) aquifers (the
  aquifer item of this list, which also covers the Yellow fallback);
  (5) regenerate the planet in the same slot (whole new body from a
  derived sub-seed, never an edit); (6) adapt the system (6a place the
  zone planet in the outer part of the zone, 6b move or remove a giant
  that blocks the slot); (7) add a brighter, heavier primary (Boss, 7:23
  PM EDT, correcting the earlier companion idea): the failing red dwarf
  system is kept unchanged (stars, planets, moons, belts, ids) and
  becomes the secondary of a WIDE binary; the new primary gets its own
  planets and the habitable steps run on its zone; repeat once for a
  third star; wide-binary stability (separation floor from both systems'
  reach, S-type limit, triple rule) is part of the step; the main new
  code is a member-tree mode that adds a primary above an existing
  system, plus designation changes (A becomes B); (8) regenerate the star
  (the last resort; a failing M dwarf is redrawn up to N times; a failing
  G or K star keeps its star and goes to step 9 unless Boss wants those
  redrawn); (9) give up with the best result found, Yellow if Suitability
  allows, recorded as unmet or fallback, never silently. Each step has an attempt cap and a seed per
  (step, attempt); suggested caps K1 8, K2 6, K3 6, K4 1, K5 6, K6 4
  each, K7 4 per added primary, K8 8 stars (design values), and a budget of attempts per request
  so a directed sector cannot run for ever. The outcome records the step
  reached and how many star draws it took. Design:
  /mnt/project-files/design-drafts/red-dwarf-water-and-star-regeneration-2026-10-23.md
  (section a, the honest note on 6c: a companion cannot make the host
  heavier or brighter, so it helps little for lost water). Done: a
  forced request is met by a Blue or Green world, or by the stated
  fallback, in every one of 120 forced systems that has an ecosphere (the
  proposal measured 7 of 120 before), the step reached is counted per
  request, the draws are deterministic across worker counts, and a
  request that cannot be met names the failing domain and the step.
  Decided (Boss, 6:39 PM EDT 2026-10-23, relayed by the coordinator):
  'there is no recalculation never redraws composition rule, at least I
  don't remember one' (bulk-composition.md decision 31 / F10 was a lane
  default, not Boss's rule; it does not block this item).
  Prerequisites: none. Related: GEN.643, GEN.646.
  Error condition (Boss, 6:54 PM EDT 2026-10-23): the request aims for a
  PHI-6 overall of Blue or Green; if it MUST, a Yellow overall is
  accepted as technically habitable so long as the sustainability factor
  (read as the Suitability domain: water within reach, food, shelter) is
  at least Yellow. The rebuilds and restricted draws aim at Blue or
  Green first; the Yellow fallback is taken only after the stated cap on
  tries and the result is marked as a fallback in its description. Food
  comes from the Flora and Fauna scores (GEN.653).
  Step 4 of the ladder is GEN.654 (aquifers, stored by DB.92).
  Step 4 of the ladder is GEN.654 (aquifers, stored by DB.92).
  Boss 5:49 PM EDT 10-30 (2026-10-30 5:50 PM EDT): Superseded in part:
  the request is a probability tweak only and never forces (see

- [ ] **GEN.752 Climate feedback on the surface temperature fixed point: ice-albedo, water vapour and cloud albedo**
  The GEN.422 fixed point of surface temperature and pressure has no
  climate feedback. Add the three feedbacks that move it: ice-albedo
  (ice cover grows as the planet cools and raises the albedo), water
  vapour (a warmer ocean world holds more vapour and warms further, with
  the runaway limit of GEN.639) and cloud albedo (cloud cover changes
  the reflected share). Each is a physical law with a published source;
  each stand-in it touches records its source tier and tweak level in
  the gap plan registry (GEN.725). The test runs the fixed point on a
  cooling and a warming sweep of a planet and checks it converges, stays
  inside the published range of Earth's climate sensitivity, and gives
  the snowball and runaway thresholds the literature gives. Found by the
  physics fix plan thread (reports/physics-fix-plan-2026-10-24.md
  section 12). Owner: pool (first free lane after 8.1 closes, unless
  Boss lets 8.4 start earlier).
  Prerequisites: GEN.462. Related: GEN.639, GEN.684, GEN.725,, GEN.972, GEN.973, GEN.974, GEN.975.
  GEN.726.

- [ ] **GEN.842 Follow-ups to elliptical orbits, tidal heating and planet spin: the approximations GEN.727, GEN.737 and GEN.731 left**
  Reported by Math 2 (as the lane reported 10:18 AM EDT 2026-10-28,
  #3380, epoch 113). Left as known approximations: (1) giant_draw.py and
  mixture_subject.py still use the semi-major axis for flux, not the
  mean-flux of the real ellipse; (2) no moon-on-planet tide, no
  atmospheric tide, no Q(T) (Q does not vary with temperature); (3)
  rogue planets keep the old day law; (4) birth days are 2 to 3 hours

  and (3) as code, and decide (2) and (4) with Boss by option card
  before building. Done: flux uses the mean flux everywhere, rogue

  letter, a class list or a body-type list (for example the A and M veto

- [ ] **GEN.918 The phenomena census uses a reference galaxy that is not Milky Way-like (bulge heavier than disk, history and density disagree by 1.57x); give it a Milky Way-like shape so GEN.900, GEN.901, GEN.902 are judged on the right galaxy (a test-harness fix, no generator change)**
  BOSS DECIDED (3:02 PM EDT 2026-10-29), card answer option 1 'following
  physics as much as possible': fix the root, no per-constant tuning.
  Found by Bug 1 (report
  /mnt/project-files/reports/bug1/star-count-normalisation-2026-10-29.md):
  the disk history (GEN.469) implies 1.65 Msun/yr now, about 2.8e8 young
  stars and 366,000 living stars of 8 Msun or more; the census galaxy
  holds 1.30e8 and 170,000, a factor 2.17 low, and the old and
  intermediate stars are low by about the same. Applying 2.17 lands
  every miss: Wolf-Rayet 580 to 1,260 (target 943 to 1,714), neutron
  stars 3.77e8 to 8.2e8 (observed about 1e9), supernova remnants 256 to
  555 (target 400 to 5,000), magnetars 21 to 46. The density model is
  anchored on local systems per cubic parsec while the history counts
  stars formed. Do: make the model's star count follow its own history
  by scaling the stars per system or the density anchor from observed
  physics (the multiplicity statistics and the local stellar density),

  clearance ledger. Where we think it belongs (best guess, can move):

  Rogue train 8 (Boss, 4:57 PM EDT) (2026-10-30 4:59 PM EDT): Boss,
  4:57 PM EDT 2026-10-30: rogue planets are all physics, each has its
  own moon system and moon compositions, and a rogue planet is
  functionally and programmatically identical to a planet in a system
  except that it carries a note that it is rogue and is not orbiting a
  star. So the rogue path calls the same planet and moon generation (the
  one body chain of GEN.557), not a simplified one; the flat-rate rogue
  tables are deleted. This item is the core of train 19: epoch with
  --affects, migration, golden refresh through Bug 2. The fields
  (GEN.1103 and GEN.1104) move to train 8 and GEN.1105 to GEN.1107 to
  train 8.
  Boss idea, 5:03 PM EDT (each star donates rogues) (2026-10-30 5:04 PM
  EDT): Boss: have each star system in a sector donate rogue planets:
  they are generated as part of the system, with a slot and a full
  history (formation, migration, moons, composition, age), then ejected,
  and the rogue keeps that history. This item is exactly that: the donor
  system builds the planet in its architecture slot, the ejection event
  is recorded in the system history, and the rogue row is the same
  planet with the rogue note, its kept moons and the ejection speed and
  age. Open question for Boss, taken as the default until he answers: an
  ejected planet drifts (speed times age: a few km/s over Gyr is
  kiloparsecs, far larger than a sector), so which sector holds it?
  Default (recommended): the rogue is stored in its donor system's
  sector, its object ID carries the parent system ID and a rank, and its
  drawn position is the parent position (young ejections) or the parent
  position displaced by the drift clamped to the sector (old ones);
  nothing moves between sectors and every sector stays independent. The
  alternative is to place it where it actually drifted, which needs the
  donors of every sector within the drift radius and breaks sector
  independence (not recommended).
  Storage sector OPEN, research first (Boss, 5:06 PM EDT) (2026-10-30
  5:07 PM EDT): Boss wants the storage question researched before it is
  decided. His proposal: compute the planet's true galactic velocity
  (its orbital velocity in the system relative to the star plus the
  system's own motion through the galaxy), eject it along a random
  direction normal to that motion vector, choose the ejection time, and
  run time forward from there to get its present position and sector. A
  research thread is on it. The home-sector default above is only a
  placeholder; build nothing that depends on where a rogue is stored
  until the research decision is merged.
  Drift research (D4, 5:12 PM EDT) (2026-10-30 5:11 PM EDT): Research
  result: storage by virtual donors. The sector draws its own ejection
  events from donor records (class, seed, distance, age, speed, slot; no
  donor system is stored or enumerated), applies the kick in the host's
  own frame, then the host's motion, then the closed form for position
  and velocity (GEN.1114, the drift function), and the rogue is placed
  in the sector where it lands; its object ID is built from the present
  galactic position, so it needs no change. This replaces "counted with
  the sector's stars" and "ejection speed is escape speed plus the
  host's velocity". HELD until Boss answers two questions: (1) virtual
  donors, recommended, or real donors only (wrong positions); (2) kick
  isotropic in the star's frame, recommended, or perpendicular to the
  galactic motion as he first proposed (that keeps rogues within a few
  hundred pc of the donor, the research shows the along-orbit component
  is what causes the long drift). The earlier home-sector default is
  superseded.
  Held also for the storage study (Boss, 5:15 PM EDT) (2026-10-30 5:17
  PM EDT): Boss proposes one galaxy-wide object store generated in
  region work units, with sectors as a navigation table (design study
  GEN.1118). The rogue storage question is part of that study; GEN.1111
  stays held until it is read.

  5:29 PM EDT 2026-10-30: (1) rogues come only from generated systems
  (each donor system builds the planet in its architecture slot, then

  mantle cap by mass (Guimond: 2 to 8 oceans) in one epoch, report the
