- [ ] **GEN.1175 Porosity weakening of body strength from a sourced law instead of the placeholder exponential**
  The engine's porosity rule is 'none' (RN5, L3) and an 'exponential'
  rule (strength times exp(-b x porosity), b 4 to 7) is built and off,
  resting on recalled ceramics coefficients; Pohl and Britt
  2020 find no usable porosity trend in meteorites and with the
  exponential on Proteus (porous, ice-rich, 210 km, not round) comes out
  round. Find a rock-mechanics or ceramics source (Grott 2019 Ryugu
  boulders at 200 to 280 kPa are a whole-body data point), choose the
  law, and register it in GEN.725 with tier and tweak level. Owner Aux
  5. Source: reports/planetary-material-strength-2026-10-31.md section
  9. Additive to the roundness engine (physics/roundness.py, GEN.1158,
  merged); no generation output changes until GEN.1159 to GEN.1162 wire
  it, so lock-free until then.
  Sources 1 finding
  (reports/strength-followup-gen1180-gen1175-2026-10-31.md) (2026-10-30
  11:33 PM EDT): One fitted law found, strength times (1 - phi/0.5)^1.67
  from Alomari, Ng and Khatri 2025, from a summary only, so the paper
  must be read; it sits inside the placeholder's b 4 to 7 band for
  porosity 0.1 to 0.4. It is a carbonate rock law: ice-rich bodies have
  no sourced porosity law. Boss uploads that matter: Alomari 2025 (open
  access, mdpi.com/1996-1944/18/6/1211) and Yamashita, Kato and Arakawa
  2010 (Icarus 207:972). Keep open until the Alomari paper is read.
  Boss uploads read (Sources 1) (9:38 AM EDT 2026-10-31, as Sources 1
  reported): Alomari, Ng and Khatri 2025 (Materials 18:1211, doi
  10.3390/ma18061211) is CONFIRMED: UCS = 60.251 (1 - 0.02 n)^1.67 MPa
  with n in percent, which is (1 - phi/n*)^1.67 with n* = 0.5 assumed,
  not fitted; also E = 30.31 (1 - 0.02 n)^1.82 GPa. Data: 178 training
  and 75 test points, porosity 0.4 to 50 percent, carbonate rocks and
  gypsum, uniaxial, no ice. Relative strength at phi 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4
  is 0.69, 0.43, 0.22, 0.07, inside our exponential b 4 to 7 band (the
  paper lists exponentials with b 4.8 to 9.3). Register as T3 (right
  form, wrong material) at tweak L1. Report:
  reports/uploaded-ice-rock-papers-check-2026-10-31.md.
  Prerequisites: none. Related: GEN.1158, GEN.725.

  Boss uploads read (Sources 1) (9:38 AM EDT 2026-10-31, as Sources 1
  reported): Goldsby and Kohlstedt 1997 (Scripta Mater. 37:1399-1406)
  read: dislocation n 4, Q 64; grain-boundary sliding n 1.8, grain
  exponent 1.4, Q 49; basal-limited n 2.4, Q 55 to 62. The GBS and basal
  Mitri 2010 numbers are now verified; the Mitri diffusion row is not in
  this paper. No prefactor A in the text (it is in Goldsby and Kohlstedt
  2001, JGR 106:11017, not in hand). Morison, Labrosse and Choblet 2021
  (Nature 600:419): N2 ice n = 2.1 (Yamashita 2010, Icarus 207:972,
  confirmed; correct an earlier 2.2), Q 3.5 kJ/mol non-Newtonian or 8.6
  kJ/mol Newtonian (Eluszkiewicz and Stevenson 1990), viscosity 1e10
  (non-Newtonian) to 1e16 to 1e19 Pa s (diffusion), 1e16 to 1e17 from
  pit relaxation. Still needed: Goldsby and Kohlstedt 2001, Durham,
  Kirby and Stern 1993 (JGR 98:17667) and Durham, Kirby and Stern 1997
  (JGR 102:16293, for ice types IT1 to IT3). The 'Rheology of Water and
  Ammonia-Water Ices' upload is only the 1993 LPSC abstract with no
  constants.
  Sources 1 read Goldsby and Kohlstedt 2001 (2026-10-31 9:47 AM EDT):
  Boss uploaded the paper; Sources 1 read Table 5 from the page image
  (report
  /mnt/project-files/reports/goldsby-2001-and-durham-planetary-ices-2026-10-31.md).
  Rate = A sigma^n d^-p exp(-Q/RT), sigma in MPa, d in metres.
  Grain-boundary-sliding-accommodated basal slip, T under 255 K: A
  3.9e-3 MPa^-1.8 m^1.4 s^-1, n 1.8, p 1.4, Q 49 kJ/mol (T over 255 K: A
  3.0e26, Q about 192). Basal-slip-accommodated GBS: A 5.5e7 MPa^-2.4
  s^-1, n 2.4, Q 60. Dislocation creep, T under 258 K: A 4.0e5 MPa^-4
  s^-1, n 4, Q 60 (T over 258 K: A 6.0e28, Q about 181). Combination:
  diffusion + (1/basal + 1/GBS)^-1 + dislocation. Mitri's GBS and basal
  log A match exactly, so those two are verified. The diffusion row is
  derived (Eq. 4 volume term at about 260 K), not measured, and the
  boundary D0 of about 6e-4 m2/s is an estimate (upper bounds 5.8e-4 to
  8.4e-4). The paper has no melt law or melting curves. The authors
  print only initials (D. L. Goldsby, D. L. Kohlstedt). Also read: the
  Durham, Kirby and Stern 1996 preprint Rheology of Planetary Ices
  (UCRL-JC-123734); its Table 1 has the 1993 ammonia dihydrate law (log
  A 21.55, n 5.81, E* 107.5 kJ/mol, tested 130 to 176 K). The dihydrate
  to ice I strength ratio is 1.7 at 135 K, 0.91 at 143 K, 0.57 at 150 K,
  0.18 at 170 K and 0.14 at 176 K (1e-15 per s; Sources 1 corrected the
  first figures, which used the preprint's ice I row below 195 K; the
  1997 row, log A -3.8, n 6.0, E* 39, is the right one). Our IT6 point at
  170 K (0.3) is above the law, 135 K (1.0) is below it, and 110 K (2.0)
  is outside the tested range. Ice II, III, V and VI constants are
  already held in Durham, Kirby and Stern 1997 Table 2 (same as the 1996
  preprint; Durham, Stern and Kirby 1996 JGR 101:2989 confirms V and VI);
  Echelmeyer and Kamb 1986 (GRL 13:693) gives ice II about 10 times ice
  I viscosity and ice III about 0.01 times near 240 K. The high-pressure
  ratios depend strongly on depth: at lab rate ice II, V and VI come out
  1 to 2 times ice I and ice III 0.4 to 0.6, at 1e-15 per s ice II, V and
  VI 3 to 7. The ice VI row above 250 K jumps 50 times across 250 K, so
  do not use it as it stands. Not found: Choukroun and Grasset 2007 and
  the solid-solid boundary equations. Melting curves are covered by
  Wagner 2011. Report: reports/ice-high-pressure-sources-held-2026-10-31.md.
  Sources 1: solid-solid ice boundaries from a tertiary source
  (2026-10-31 10:03 AM EDT): Choukroun and Grasset 2007 cannot be had
  (Boss cannot get it), so the boundaries below 0.7 GPa come from one
  TERTIARY source: Martin Chaplin, Water Phase Diagram, water.lsbu.ac.uk
  (updated 5 Nov 2021; its references are by number only and the list is
  unreachable). Register them in GEN.725 as tier Unverified (T3), L0,
  until a paper matches. P in MPa, T in K, d = T - 273.15: Ih-II 176.0 +
  0.918 (T - 198.15); II-III 213 + 99.517 [(T/238.45)^19.676 - 1]; II-V
  412.0 - 7.01 (T - 239.15); Ih-III 198.2 - 0.42 (T - 273.15) (the
  quadratic version fails its own triple point, 166 against 209.9, do
  not use); III-V 344.3 - 0.275 d - 0.01099 d^2; V-VI 625.9 + 0.06086 d
  - 0.0008571 d^2. Triple points: L-Ih-III 251.165 K, 209.9 MPa; L-III-V
  256.164 K, 350.1 MPa; L-V-VI 273.31 K, 632.4 MPa (Wagner 2011, also
  Journaux et al. arXiv 1907.09598 Table 4); Ih-II-III 238.45 K, 212.9
  MPa; II-III-V 248.85 K, 344.3 MPa; II-V-VI about 218 K, 620 MPa
  (approximate; the printed II-V line gives 559 there, so do not extend
  a line past its triple points); VI-VII-L 2216 MPa, 355 K. Sources 1
  checked that every line meets its triple points within 1 MPa except
  III-V at the liquid point (345.8 against 350.1). Chaplin's short Simon
  form for ice VII melting is 10 percent off at 550 K: use the exact
  IAPWS form already held. AQUA (A&A 2020, arXiv 2009.10098) Eq. 22
  gives a VI-VII fit; the extraction is garbled, verify before use. No
  equation found for II-VI, VI-VII-VIII or VII-VIII. Fortes 2009 (J.
  Appl. Cryst. 42:846) says Choukroun and Grasset's ice Ih K0' is wrong
  by 10 times and their ice VI density has no pressure term, so do not
  trust their equation of state for volumes. Still missing: Dunaeva 2010
  (Solar System Research 44:202) or Choukroun and Grasset by upload.
  Report: reports/ice-phase-boundaries-secondary-sources-2026-10-31.md.
  Prerequisites: none. Related: GEN.1183, GEN.1185, GEN.725.

- [ ] **GEN.1194 Runaway greenhouse: the radiative-convective model has no plateau in outgoing flux, so water window opacity, continuum temperature dependence and wings must be reworked until it plateaus**
  From Air 1 (GEN.973 finding): outgoing flux rises monotonically with
  temperature in the radiative-convective model (343 W/m2 at 330 K
  saturated against Simpson and Nakajima's plateau near 280), and the
  fixed point stays near 320 K at 320 W/m2 absorbed with no step through
  350 K, so a runaway-threshold test against GEN.639 cannot pass as a
  model-behaviour test. The fix is not new feedback code but different
  opacity: the water window opacity, the continuum's temperature
  dependence and the line wings, so the outgoing flux plateaus near 280
  W/m2. The same too-steep slope explains the sweep's low sensitivity
  (model Earth twin about 0.43 K per W/m2 against the 0.54 bound; the
  missing ice-albedo +0.4 and cloud +0.4 W/m2 per K feedbacks close the
  gap by the AR6 budget). Register changed stand-ins in GEN.725, then
  add the runaway-threshold test (converges below the limit, runs away
  above it). Output changes, an epoch with GEN.972 if the train allows.
  Owner Air 1.
  Prerequisites: none. Related: GEN.973, GEN.639, GEN.972, GEN.974,
  GEN.725.

  GEN.1216 research done (Sources 1, 3:25 PM UTC lane clock) (2026-10-31
  11:35 AM EDT): report
  /mnt/project-files/reports/gen1216-surface-liquid-composition-2026-10-31.md.
  Headline: every liquid family has anchors but no published closed law
  of composition against conditions, so the generator must build the law
  (solubility, saturation, equilibrium) and use the anchors as checks.
  Sourced: TEOS-10 seawater ion table; Mars perchlorate and chloride
  eutectics (Marion 2010, Toner 2014); Enceladus Na-Cl-CO3 at pH 11 to
  12 and Europa MgSO4 1.1 to 96.8 g/kg; H2SO4-H2O eutectics 211 K at 36
  wt percent and 199 K at 38; ammonia-water eutectic 176 K at 33 wt
  percent plus 7 liquidus points; CO2 triple point and saturated density
  and viscosity (Span and Wagner, Fenghour); Titan seas CH4 71 to 80, N2
  17 to 20, C2H6 0 to 12 mol percent against a model spread of 10 times.
  Stand-ins checked: CO2 viscosity at 220 K is 21 percent low; MgSO4
  eutectic 1.2 K low; NaClO4 3 K low; sulfur melting 388.4 should be 392
  K; ammonia-water viscosity and density off 2 to 6 times; ammonia share
  0.1 is the top of the comet to disc range. Life: water limits sourced
  (pH -0.06 to 12.5, water activity 0.611 to 0.635, ionic strength about
  10 mol/L, MgCl2 about 2.3 M); nothing for acid above a few percent,
  ammonia above about 1.6 percent, or CO2 or hydrocarbon as a solvent,
  so classes 5 to 9 stay at the lowest tiers (T8 or T9, L3 or L4).
  Questions answered (2026-10-31 11:58 AM EDT): Boss answered (11:56 AM
  EDT 2026-10-31): (1) yes, a body may hold one extra liquid beside its
  main one; (2) store a liquid's makeup as separate columns; (3) acid

  stand-in, also to be tuned from physics and chemistry (same research);
  (6) a body with methane and carbon monoxide ice warm enough for liquid
  methane gets a methane sea.
  Question 3 answered (2026-10-31 12:01 PM EDT): Boss answered question
  3 (11:57 AM EDT 2026-10-31): option 1, store sulfuric acid clouds too,
  the strongest level with a pool-or-cloud flag. This replaces the
  earlier note that cloud storage waited for an answer; all six surface

  Boss asked for the ammonia gate and nitrogen ice amount to be tuned
  from physics (2026-10-31 12:40 PM EDT): GEN.1225 research done by
  Sources 1 (as the lane reported), report
  /mnt/project-files/reports/gen1225-ammonia-gate-and-nitrogen-ice-2026-10-31.md
  (stand-in table in section 4). Ammonia gate: the earlier 1 to 1.6
  percent figure was an arithmetic error; 1500 to 7000 mg N/L is 0.18 to
  0.85 wt percent NH3; the highest reported growth in solution is about
  0.7 to 0.9 wt percent and nothing near 10 percent exists, so class 8
  is pure inference. The 10 percent only has meaning as antifreeze
  (liquidus 259.6 K, 13 K below water). Proposed gate: ammonia share at
  least the liquidus share for the body's temperature (5 percent at 267
  K, 14 at 251, 20 at 235), upper bound the 33 percent peritectic, with
  a note that no measurement exists above 0.9 wt percent; replaces LF44
  (T9 L4) with T3 L1 for the gate, the life statement stays T9 L4.
  Nitrogen ice: N2 condenses only below the partial-pressure temperature
  (22 to 30 K, 28 K at 1e-4 bar; add to CS1 ICE_CONDENSATION_K); the
  solar ceiling N2/H2O is 0.107 by mass but observed cold bodies hold
  1e-4 to 1.4e-3 (67P, Pluto) through trapping in amorphous ice; the 2
  percent used in the retention papers is 15 to 170 times too high.
  Proposed GN1 trapping 0.001 to 0.013 of the ceiling (T3 L2), GN2
  retention stays T8 L4. Touches LF62 (NH3 share 0.1, top of range), IS1
  and CS1. Build these as registered stand-ins (GEN.725, with burn-down
  lines for any L3/L4 row).
  Prerequisites: none. Related: GEN.1215, GEN.1207, GEN.862.

- [ ] **GEN.1228 Hematite (the oxidised ground type) reflects the same in all three bands, so a rusty world renders dark grey instead of red; give it a sourced spectrum or finer bands (bug)**
    Finding from Aux 4's MAP.274 build (as the lane reported, 12:52 PM
  EDT 2026-10-31).
    The materials table's hematite_fine reflectance is flat across the
  three bands the land colour reads (0.092 at 450 nm, 0.086 at 550 nm,
  0.085 at 650 nm), so ground that is mostly oxidised iron renders dark
  grey, where real hematite dust is red because it reflects far more at
  650 nm than at 450 nm. Fix: a sourced hematite spectrum, or finer
  bands in the table (written in docs/design/interface/body-rendering.md
  section 4.1). Changes the colour of oxidised worlds on the map and
  body pages only; no stored generator value moves. Lock-free (the
  land colour, MAP.274, has merged).
  Prerequisites: none.

  replaces the fall speed, and the aggregate cross section). Do: derive
  the depth per unit of mass flux from the physics (sourced), fix the

- [ ] **GEN.1230 The disc star formation history should decline to the present for a Milky Way mass galaxy: the model gives 0.49 to 0.55 of the ten Gy mean, measured is 0.20 to 0.3 (bug)**
  Found by Core 3 while closing TEST.533 (#4575, 2:55 PM EDT 10-31 as
  the lane reported). Present star formation over its ten-Gy mean for
  the model disc is 0.49 (0.55 after GEN.999) against 0.20 to 0.3
  measured for the Milky Way (Licquia and Newman 2015). Cause is not the
  gas law: the inflow in disk_history follows the halo's stellar growth,
  and for a light halo that rises to the present, while the Milky Way's
  own history declines. Measured for the test's disc by halo mass:
  1.0e12 gives 0.89, 1.6e12 0.49, 2.0e12 0.39, 3.1e12 0.29. GEN.1154
  lowered the median halo of a 5e10 galaxy from 2.0e12 to 1.57e12 solar
  masses. Candidate causes: the inflow shape (halo growth rate against
  the stellar-to-halo relation) and the thin disc's age. Physics
  decides, no game rate; any stand-in goes in GEN.725 with tier and
  level. TEST.533 widened the bound to a factor of three with the reason
  in the test; tighten it back when this lands. Interacts with GEN.999
  (adds 10 percent), so look at it after train 8. Lock work (epoch).
  Related: GEN.999, GEN.1154, GEN.1200, GEN.1202. Owner: Core 3.
  Prerequisites: none.

- [ ] **GEN.1233 Dust rings fed by small moons (Jupiter, Uranus, Neptune): a steady-state supply so giants with faint rings are not left ringless by the ring lifetime law**
  From Tides 1 (relayed 5:06 PM EDT 2026-10-31 as the lane reported),
  the follow-up of GEN.1171: the ring lifetime law (viscous spreading
  plus meteoroid erosion) correctly kills a ring that has no supply, but
  dust rings that small moons and impacts keep feeding (Jupiter's,
  Uranus's and Neptune's rings, steady-state) are not modelled, so
  giants with 4 of 4 rings in the Solar System now come out ringed about
  9 percent of the time. Do: a supply term for rings near small moons
  (impact ejecta from meteoroid flux on the moons' surfaces, with a
  yield and a loss time from the same erosion and drag laws), so a faint
  dust ring persists where a moon feeds it; the Solar System rings are
  tests, not anchors; every stand-in goes in GEN.725 with tier and tweak
  level. Done: the ringed share of giants moves toward the observed
  share of giants with rings (all four in the Solar System, with the
  sample caveat) by the physics, the census is printed before and after.
  Changes stored ring columns, so it rides a train. Owner: Tides 1.
  Prerequisites: none. Related: GEN.1171, GEN.725.

- [ ] **PERF.72 Research the cost of a sector's gravity grid and where to cut between exact and aggregated sources**
  Done: a note (docs/design/orbits/gravity-map.md, section 'How it is
  computed', extended with measurements) says what a grid of 16 zones
  per edge costs for a dense sector (core, bulge and arm) and a sparse
  one, with numpy and the per-region aggregates of MAP.151, picks the
  near/far distance and the zone count, gives the error of the aggregate
  against the exact sum, and says when a grid is recomputed after an
  orbital update (every step, or only for sectors whose sources moved by
  a set amount). Ends with the build items filed.
  Math Research (2026-10-14): the field is a sum over point masses at many
  grid points, the same shape as the path integrator's acceleration; cost it
  as a numba or NumPy kernel from the start (not measured in the note).
  Prerequisites: GEN.198. Related: GEN.198, GEN.199, MAP.151
  (done, PR #1539).
  Scope after the review (2026-10-16 review): the cost study of the grid
  on top of the kernel (measure the kernel and the aggregate split, pick
  the near and far distance and the zone count, state the error); no

- [ ] **PERF.129 Robust tile caching: the first zoom levels built ahead, tiles stored compressed, built proactively around every visit, kept until the data changes**
  Boss, 2026-10-17, 4:31 PM EDT: "for 8.2 I want to add robust tile
  caching, so that we build out not only the initial galactic view but
  all the normal zoom levels for that view that we can compress and
  serve up to the client immediately on request. Basically I want to
  build out tiles for the first several zoom levels and then I want to
  build it so that system is proactive and when the user visits and zoom
  level it builds and caches all the surrounding tiles and the next zoom
  levels. Then it keeps them until the data changes." What exists (read
  from main, 2026-10-17): `web/lib/tilecache.py` keeps packed tiles on
  disk (`<cache dir>/<db>/<generation>/<tile>.bin`, the PGT1 format of
  `tilepack.py`), answers `/galaxy/tiles` by joining stored bytes, and
  keeps stage and window payloads the same way; freshness is the content
  stamp plus `GET /api/galaxy/changes` (the `modified_at` columns, so
  only the changed tiles are deleted, and a change that cannot be pinned
  to tiles starts a new generation); `prune` deletes the least recently
  written files above `tile_cache.max_mb`; the browser keeps its own
  copy in IndexedDB (MAP.158); `web/warmup.py` warms only the opening
  view's tiles and the galaxy stage; Apache compresses each response at
  send time; the admin health block shows where the cache lives and its
  size. Goal (done when its subitems are): the Galaxy Map answers any
  tile of the first several zoom levels at once from a stored compressed
  copy; a visit to any zoom level builds and caches the surrounding
  tiles and the next level's tiles before they are asked for; every
  stored tile stays until the data under it changes; and an admin can
  see and clear the cache. Subitems: PERF.130 (build the first levels
  ahead), PERF.131 (store and serve compressed), PERF.132 (proactive
  neighbours and next levels on a visit), PERF.133 (keep until the data
  changes), PERF.134 (admin: see and clear). It touches PERF.41 (the
  TILE_FORMAT stamp: a format change must drop the stored tiles once),
  MAP.239 (the tile root rises to the reach, which changes every level's
  geometry, so the build waits for it), MAP.195 (finer tiles leave out
  what a coarser tile sent, which changes what a tile holds), PERF.127
  (`planetgen warm`: the tile build is one of its families, each its own
  command, PERF.120), and the plan commands (a regenerated galaxy
  changes tile content, so the build is a step the wrapper lists after
  the generation commands, never a part of one). Owner: Core 2
  (proposed; the map and cache lane).
  Owner: none for now, returned to the pool (Boss, 7:44 PM EDT
  2026-10-22: work outside 8.1 is paused until 8.1 is complete; Core 2
  held it before; this replaces any earlier owner line).
  Prerequisites: PERF.134.
  Related: PERF.41, PERF.104, PERF.120, PERF.127, MAP.158, MAP.159,
  MAP.195, MAP.239.
  Cut order (Boss, 2026-10-17, 6:48 PM EDT, MAP.250, Decided): the tiles
  stored here are built with halo and satellite-galaxy stars ranked
  below every other star, so a budget cut removes them first; landing
  that rule bumps the tile cache stamp and the cached tiles are rebuilt
  once. The galaxy map lag Boss reported at the same time is MAP.249; if
  its cause is the missing cache, this item is brought forward.
  Boss (2026-10-18, 5:43 PM EDT) widened this goal: the warm-up after
  every update, generation or change runs in phases and goes as deep as
  it can; the stored data may be about 10 times the 40 MB the first tile
  cache cost; the cache is capped at 1 GB by a setting (`cache.max_mb`,
  a slider on the settings page and a key in `config.json`); and every
  list of the site gets a cached index that regenerates when its data
  changes. Filed as PERF.139 (the setting), ADM.97 (the slider),
  PERF.141 (the phased warm-up) and, as one goal with the index and
  lists, DB.79, PERF.140 and UX.141 (issue #2293). Full wording on
  PERF.139.
  Contradiction sweep (Boss's request, 2026-10-18, 5:44 PM EDT; the
  newer note wins, report todo-contradictions-2026-10-18.md): "brought
  forward if its cause is the missing cache" is superseded by Boss's
  card on MAP.249 (2026-10-18, about 8:54 AM EDT, "Both, cut payload
  first"): the tile cache work follows MAP.249's payload cut.
  Decided (Boss, tapped "Skip it" on the card "Store Galaxy Map tiles
  compressed (PERF.131), or skip it?" at 11:27 AM EDT 2026-10-21, tap
  verified on the platform): PERF.131 is skipped and retired. Apache
  keeps compressing at send time (Core 2 measured under 0.1 s a big
  view: a 200-tile view is 3.8 MB packed and 0.8 MB gzipped, gzip 0.03
  to 0.10 s, against 3 to 54 s to build a cold view) and PERF.132
  (#2298) removed the real waits; no new wire format.

- [ ] **PERF.166 The mean-system-mass lookup bisects per age (0.2 ms each); a faster form changes the last bits and needs an epoch and Boss's word (bug)**
  Found by the Performance lane in PERF.163 (merged as #2576, relayed
  10:25 PM EDT 2026-10-22 as the lane reported); Boss's live observation
  of the 264 s plan stage, so a bug. PERF.163 raised the
  mean-system-mass cache from 512 to 65,536 ages (a plan asks for about
  22,000); `plan --mass 4e9` fell from about 2 minutes (8.0.1960) to
  about 30 s after PERF.146 and about 25 s now, and the plan log ends
  with a step table. The per-age bisection in the mean-system-mass

  it with a closed form or an interpolation table would change the last

  generator epoch (numbered at merge) and Boss's word, and goes to a
  later version unless he says otherwise. Do: measure what the bisection
  costs now (the lane's table says it is small after the cache fix), and
  only if it is worth it, design the replacement with the error bound
  stated and the golden outputs re-baselined. Done: either the measured
  cost is on this item and Boss agrees to leave it, or the replacement
  is merged with its epoch. Owner: none for now (needs Boss's word;
  pool).
  Decided (Boss, 12:27 PM EDT 2026-10-23 (cards, relayed by the
  coordinator)): leave it, option 1. No epoch is spent; the item moves
  to the version 'later' page, phase 3, and is built only if a later

- [ ] **PERF.224 Cheaper bright-table bound: fewer compositions per bin, so the star tables build about 1.7 times faster**
  From Star 2 (relayed 5:05 PM EDT 2026-10-31 as the lane reported):
  since GEN.1024 (train 7) a table's per-cell bound reads five
  compositions of the bin (was three), each on both branches' tracks
  (thin and alpha-rich) wherever the age window reaches the thick disc,
  so about ten distinct tracks per cell against three. One table build
  (old population, solar bin) takes 7.0 s against 2.3 s before at 100
  solar luminosities, and 3.3 s against 0.9 s at 2500;
  test_backfilled_cells_get_band_stars_in_their_own_cell takes about 12
  minutes. The cost is spread over MIST lookups
  (main_sequence_bright_from_gy 54 percent), nothing hot to cache, and
  memoising was tried for PERF.218 (3 to 28 percent). Do: bound each bin
  with three compositions per branch, or the minimum and maximum of the
  bin, about 1.7 times faster; this changes which draws are rejected, so

- [ ] **PERF.226 Every generation stage has a measured worker memory, and the worker cap uses it, so no stage past the scatter can run the host out of memory**
  Boss (2026-10-31, 6:01 PM EDT, as the coordinator relayed): the

  host; every other stage uses the ordinary 300 MB per worker guess
  (`WORKER_MEMORY_MB`) and 60 percent of the host (`HOST_MEMORY_SHARE`),
  which nobody has measured. A run that dies three hours in is more
  likely a later stage (bright-star units, system fill, planets,
  phenomena) than a scatter. Do: (1) read the failed run's log for the
  last stage line and the host's kernel log for the process the killer
  chose and its resident size, and say which stage it was; (2) measure
  the peak resident memory of one worker of every stage kind on a
  populated database (a run with a memory sampler, or
  `resource.getrusage` at the end of each task, written to the stage's
  progress line); (3) put each stage's measured peak in
  `MEMORY_HEAVY_KINDS` (renamed for what it is) with a margin, and have
  `stage_worker_cap` apply to every stage, so a stage that grows past
  its guess is slowed, not killed; (4) print the measured peak per
  worker in the run report so the next growth shows before it kills.
  Done: a test that every command kind has a memory figure or says it is
  ordinary on purpose, and a measured run on a populated database whose
  report lists the peak per stage and finishes under the cap. Lock-free,

  worker count). Owner: Star 2 (proposed by the Train Manager, 6:03 PM EDT

  1213 a bounded number of times as the repository's other stages do,
  whichever the statements show is the cause; (3) check the other stages
  that update stored rows from several workers for the same pattern.
  Done: a test that runs two overlapping units against one database and
  finishes without error, and a populated run with 4 workers that
  finishes the stage. Lock-free, generation output unchanged. Owner:
  unassigned (Star 2 has PERF.226; a waiting lane may take it). Version
  8.1. Prerequisites: none. Related: PERF.226.

- [ ] **DB.40 Parity data backup part: the parity file of the DB repair copied into the backup archive**
  Boss (2026-10-16, 1:59 PM and 2:00 PM EDT): "let's add backups of the
  control DB and backups of the parity data for DB repair." and "All
  those should be bz2 tarballed together." Boss (2:00 PM EDT): "we also
  have to build a way to use that data so build that out and let's make
  this targetted for v9.0 so incorporate the chain for these (restore /
  repair using backups) with that due date. Settings page is v8.1".
  Target 8.9 (the backups and repair chain, umbrella ADM.91); the
  settings page and the settings backups stay in 8.1 (ADM.83 to ADM.85).
  All backup pieces are parts of one `.tar.bz2` archive (ADM.87);
  retention is `settings.backups_kept` (default 20, 1 to 200). DB.9
  keeps parity for every sector in an append-only parity file outside
  the database (path in `config.json`). A damaged database is only
  repairable with a parity file that matches it, so the file is a backup
  part, written to `parity/`: the copy is taken under the parity
  writer's lock and cuts at the last complete record (the file is an
  append-only log of self-describing records with a header scan, so no
  index is stored); it can be switched off for a very large galaxy with
  the option `settings.backup_parity` (default on), and the manifest
  records its size and the sector count it covers. Done: the part
  registered with ADM.87, the lock-held copy under a concurrent save,
  and the size and coverage in the manifest (the restore is DB.41).
  Prerequisites: none. Related: ADM.85, DB.8, DB.17.

- [ ] **DB.41 Parity data restore: put a backed-up parity file back and check it against the database**
  Boss (2:00 PM EDT): "we also have to build a way to use that data so
  build that out and let's make this targetted for v9.0 so incorporate
  the chain for these (restore / repair using backups) with that due
  date. Settings page is v8.1". Target 8.9 (the backups and repair
  chain, umbrella ADM.91); the settings page and the settings backups
  stay in 8.1 (ADM.83 to ADM.85). All backup pieces are parts of one
  `.tar.bz2` archive (ADM.87); retention is `settings.backups_kept`
  (default 20, 1 to 200). Using the parity part of an archive: restore
  writes the file back (to a temporary name first, then renamed), then
  runs the DB.8 check so every record that no longer matches the
  database is recomputed by the stale-record rule of DB.9 instead of
  being read as damage, and reports how many sectors are unprotected
  until their next save. `planetgen.cli.backup restore --part parity
  ARCHIVE` and the backup list use it. Done: a restore on a fixture
  galaxy followed by a passing check, a record from before an edit
  treated as stale and not as damage, and a refused restore while a save
  is writing parity.
  Prerequisites: DB.40. Related: DB.9, ADM.85, ADM.91.

- [ ] **DB.42 Repair the galaxy from an archive: `repair-db --from-archive` uses the parity part of a backup when the live parity file is missing or damaged**
  Boss (2:00 PM EDT): "we also have to build a way to use that data so
  build that out and let's make this targetted for v9.0 so incorporate
  the chain for these (restore / repair using backups) with that due
  date. Settings page is v8.1". Target 8.9 (the backups and repair
  chain, umbrella ADM.91); the settings page and the settings backups
  stay in 8.1 (ADM.83 to ADM.85). All backup pieces are parts of one
  `.tar.bz2` archive (ADM.87); retention is `settings.backups_kept`
  (default 20, 1 to 200). The galaxy database itself is not in the
  archive (too large; it can be regenerated from the seed, DB.17, and
  repaired from parity, DB.9). `repair-db` of DB.9 reads the live parity
  file; with `--from-archive ARCHIVE` (or the choice on the repair page)
  it reads the archive's parity part instead when the live file is
  missing, damaged or newer than the damage. It applies the stale-record
  decision table against the live database, rebuilds every damaged
  sector it can, and lists the sectors it cannot repair (a stale record,
  more than m members of a group lost) for the seed regeneration of
  DB.17, with a report of what came from which source. Done: tests on a
  copy of a small galaxy: the live parity file deleted and the damage
  repaired from the archive, a group that lost too many members listed
  and handed to DB.17, and a stale archive recompute that does not
  damage a healthy sector.
  Prerequisites: DB.41, DB.17. Related: DB.9, DB.17, ADM.91.

- [ ] **DB.109 Optional parity follow-ups: refresh the parity file after a generation run, and keep a before-image on the edit paths so an edit is a parity delta, not a group recompute**
  Core 1's suggestion at the end of DB.46 to DB.48 (#3451, #3456,
  #3460): (1) planetgen refresh-parity runs after a generation run
  finishes when parity.enabled is on, so the file is never stale after a
  fill; (2) the edit paths (admin and the property sheet edits) keep a
  before-image of the sector so the parity updates by a delta instead of
  recomputing the whole group. Both are optional and off the critical
  path; the parity file is off by default. Owner: Core 1 when it runs
  dry.
  Prerequisites: none.

## API: The JSON API

- [ ] **API.3 Remote generate: generate on a local machine, upload through the API**
  Boss (2026-10-01 19:22Z): "using an API key add a remote-generate
  option where I can use generate.py with the right command lines to
  have my local system (much faster than the server-side) generate
  whatever I want and use the API to add it into the system once it's
  generated. Do not implement yet." Today `generate.py` writes straight
  to a MySQL/MariaDB database it can reach, and the API's write routes
  (`api/edits.py`, API.1's create-a-system route from PR #170) take one
  system or body at a time with an admin's API key. Done: `generate.py`
  gets a remote mode (for example `--remote URL --api-key KEY`) for the
  same commands and options as a local run (`sector`, `galaxy` modes,
  `plan`, the bright-star scatter and backfill, `population`); it asks
  the server for what it needs first (the galaxy's seed and skeleton,
  which sectors are already filled, the id and name state), generates
  on the local machine with all its workers, then uploads the results
  in batches to new API routes that check the key, validate each batch
  (ADM.5's validator), refuse sectors that were filled meanwhile, save
  them the same way a server-side run does (names, ids, bright-star
  levels, caches and tiles invalidated), and report what was added. A
  remote run appears in the job tree and job page (ADM.10, PR #294; ADM.12, PR #285) like
  a server-side one. Boss's answers (2026-10-01 19:28Z):
  - Generate and keep in memory: the local machine needs no database of
    its own.
  - The name indexes and id state are downloaded from the API once, for
    local use, so the run doesn't keep calling the API for them (the
    server reserves id blocks and claims the sectors for the run).
  - Uploads and downloads are compressed (gzip, bz2 or similar): some
    compression time is worth faster transfers.
  - Fully resumable: the local machine caches on disk every API call it
    means to send until the server confirms it; the server keeps a
    buffer of everything it receives, stages it, and writes to the
    database in a controlled way only complete units (a complete star
    system, a complete sector). This probably needs database changes
    so staged data can be stored and flagged incomplete until it is.
  - The local version must match the server's API version (API.4 and
    API.5).
  Boss's answers (2026-10-01 19:32Z):
  - Only an admin's API key can upload; user-level keys can read but
    never upload (API.6).
  - Upload limits are investigated and planned separately (API.7).
  - Reserved ids and claimed sectors stay reserved until the upload
    finishes or an admin clears it; nothing else may use them in the
    meantime. Admins see and clear incomplete uploads on their own page
    (ADM.13).
  - The server checks every upload and has the final say on what is
    written to the database (API.8).
  Order: API.4, API.5 and API.6 first (version and key scopes), then
  API.7's plan, then API.3's sub-items below with API.8 and ADM.13.
  Research (2026-10-09, api-design-standards.md): the upload unit is
  `StarSystem.to_dict()` objects in a versioned envelope, not table rows
  (rows named after `schema.sql` would force an API bump on nearly every
  migration). Measured 58.6 KB raw and 13.8 KB gzip per system.

  Prerequisites: API.30, ADM.95.
  - [ ] **API.10 Reservations: claimed sectors and id blocks per run**
    `id_blocks` exists (one next id per table, used by parallel
    generation) but nothing reserves sectors. Done: a run record
    holding its claimed sectors and id ranges until it finishes or an
    admin clears it (ADM.13); server-side runs and other uploads skip
    claimed sectors.
    Research (2026-10-09, api-design-standards.md): reservation on the
    existing `_allocate_id` hi/lo mechanism, with a new
    `upload_id_ranges` table and a "reserve more" call; sizes from the
    rows per system in design doc 6.1 plus 25%.
    When the claims exist, applying a change plan (ADM.60) refuses a
    sector an upload run has claimed, as server-side runs do.
    Needs the upload bookkeeping tables (first child of API.11), which
    it uses (`upload_runs`, `upload_claims`, `upload_id_ranges`)
    (2026-10-16 review). Added to Done: applying a change plan refuses a
    sector an upload run has claimed, with a test.

- [ ] **API.5 API version and compatibility checking**
  Boss (2026-10-01 19:28Z): "Another TODO item will be API version /
  compatibility checking so that we make sure the server knows how to
  take data from different client versions." Done: every API request
  carries the client's API version (a header); the server answers with
  its own version and the range it accepts (`/api/health`), refuses a
  client outside that range with a clear message saying which version
  to install, and, inside the range, reads older clients' payloads
  through converters so it knows how to take data from each supported
  version. `generate.py`'s remote mode (API.3) checks before it starts
  generating, not after. Built on API.4's compatibility data. Question
  (decided below): how many older versions the server keeps accepting.
  Research (2026-10-09, api-design-standards.md): answer "how many older
  versions": the current major, plus the previous major for one release
  cycle after a major bump, for upload payloads only (no read
  converters). Add `GET /api/version` (public, database-free, returns
  `api_version`, `min_client`, `max_client`, `release`, `version_key`,
  `galaxy_schema`) and the `PlanetGen-API-Version` header both ways;
  `generate.py --remote` checks before reading config. A refusal is `400
  api_version_unsupported` (or `410` past a sunset), not `426`; the
  check does not depend on `/api/health`. Add the version-key comparison
  (design doc 4.5). Decided (Boss, 2026-10-10 18:44Z, defaults approved;
  defaults taken): a remote
  client may differ in release within the accepted range, with a
  warning; a version-key mismatch (OS, architecture, Python) warns and
  does not refuse.
  Decided (2026-10-10): Boss (19:12Z): keep the current major plus the
  previous major for one release cycle (upload payloads only).
  Contradiction sweep (Boss's request, 2026-10-18, 5:44 PM EDT; the
  newer note wins, report todo-contradictions-2026-10-18.md): the
  version header is `X-PlanetGen-API-Version` (the code's
  `API_VERSION_HEADER`, docs/reference/api.md, API.31 of 2026-10-17, 11:33 AM
  EDT), not `PlanetGen-API-Version`; and the server reports its version
  and accepted range at `GET /api/version` (2026-10-09 research), not
  only at `/api/health`, which may keep reporting `api_version`.

- [ ] **API.6 User-level API keys, owned by the account that created them, that can read but not upload**
  Boss (2026-10-01 19:32Z): "Only admin can upload, and Admin can
  create user-level API keys that can access but not upload." Today
  API keys (`admin_api_keys`) belong to admins and carry every admin
  right. Done: an admin can create, name, list and revoke user-level
  API keys; a user-level key can use the read routes (and anything
  later granted to users) but every write route, the remote upload
  routes of API.3 above all, answers 403 for it; an admin key keeps
  every right. Ties in with USR.1 and USR.2 (user accounts and roles)
  and PR #293 (TEST.44), which already answers 403 to
  any API key that makes keys, changes credentials or 2FA, or logs
  out. Decided (Boss, 2026-10-02 01:31Z): "all keys are attached to
  the account that created them". Every API key, admin or user-level,
  records the account that created it, and requests made with it act as
  that account. Today that is an admin account; once user accounts exist
  (USR.1, USR.2) a user's keys belong to that user, so this touches the
  user account work (USR): the key-to-account link for user accounts
  builds after USR.2. Logging every call is its own item, API.15,
  which doesn't wait for user accounts.
  Research (2026-10-09, settings-seo-and-accounts.md): effective rights
  are the intersection of the key's scope and the owner's current role,
  evaluated per request (open question for Boss, default: a user-level
  key made by an admin acts as the creating account with read-only
  scope).
  Prerequisites: USR.26.

- [ ] **API.8 Verify uploaded data before it is finalized**
  Boss (2026-10-01 19:32Z): "the API will have to have a reliable method
  of syncing and making sure uploaded data is verified good before it
  is finalized in the DB, the server has the final say in how items are
  added to the database." Done: the client and server agree, by batch
  and by unit (a star system, a sector), on what has been sent and
  received, with checksums, so nothing is lost or written twice; every
  staged unit is checked on the server before it is finalized
  (complete, well formed, inside its reserved sector and id block,
  names unique, and the physics checks of ADM.5's validator); the
  server finalizes a unit in one transaction or rejects it with the
  reasons, and may correct what it can (renaming a clashing name,
  re-running derived values) rather than trusting the client's copy.
  Question (decided below): which corrections the server makes on its
  own, and
  which reject the unit so the client regenerates it.
  Research (2026-10-09, api-design-standards.md): adopt the auto-correct
  versus reject rule (design doc 7.4) as the default answer: correct
  only a clashing name and pure derived columns; reject everything else;
  the server returns a rename map; a rejection does not release the
  claim.
  Decided (2026-10-10): Boss (19:16Z, Accept all): the server auto-fixes
  only a clashing name and purely derived columns, and rejects
  everything else so the client regenerates it.
  Narrowed (2026-10-16, Boss 1:33 PM EDT): the checks, the
  one-transaction finalize and the limited auto-fix are the unit
  finalizer ADM.82, built in 8.6 for change plans. This item is what
  remains: the batch and unit sync with checksums, the staged units, and
  calling the finalizer when a unit is sealed.
  Prerequisites: ADM.82.

- [ ] **ADM.32 Add a star system to a sector: at the emptiest spot, at given coordinates, or at random outside every Hill sphere**
  Boss (2026-10-07 11:47Z): "Need a way to add a single star system to a
  sector, the computer will place in the area of lowest density if it
  can without crossing the hill sphere of another object, if the object
  cannot be placed then it will gracefully error out." And: "Add the
  ability to insert a sector or move a stand-alone sector into some
  location in a sector of admin's choosing.  They can specify
  coordinates (in 3 different ways) of the star system relative to the
  center of the sector or center of the galaxy (either needs to be an
  option).  The admin should also be able to select random placement
  within the sector so long as it is not in a hill sphere, the system
  will not move existing stars without admin approval. Admin can also
  choose to have the computer put the new star system in the least
  populated area, basically the spot that is farthest from everything
  that you can get within the sector." Done: from the sector page, an
  admin adds a new or existing stand-alone system by (1) the emptiest
  point (farthest from every object), (2) coordinates in Cartesian,
  cylindrical or spherical form relative to the sector centre or the
  galaxy centre (GEN.74), or (3) random; no placement may fall inside
  another object's Hill sphere, nothing existing moves without the admin
  confirming, and a placement that can't be made fails with a message
  and changes nothing.
  Moved to phase 3, Move and orbit, before ADM.71, and built on the
  shell and the plan engine: the action becomes the "add" plan operation
  that goes through approval; ADM.71 takes the placement functions from
  here and narrows to the move operation and the drag (2026-10-16
  review).
  Prerequisites: ADM.65, ADM.66, ADM.82.

- [ ] **ADM.60 Apply, undo and audit a plan: one job, one activity-log entry per operation**
  Boss (2026-10-16, 1:07 PM EDT), headline of 8.6 (ADM.57): the admin
  has complete control; the world adjusts to what the admin wants, after

  the unit finalizer (ADM.82). An approved plan is applied, under the
  approver's identity, as a visible queue job (the journal and the
  activity log name the requester and the approver) (the Generate page
  job log): operations run in order inside
  one transaction per sector, each writes its journal rows and an
  activity-log entry, and a failure rolls the whole plan back and leaves
  it proposed with the reason. An applied plan can be undone as long as

  changes nothing and an undo that restores every stored row.

- [ ] **ADM.61 Edits survive repair and regeneration: replay the journal after a sector is rebuilt from its seed or from parity**
  Boss (2026-10-16, 1:07 PM EDT), headline of 8.6 (ADM.57): the admin
  has complete control; the world adjusts to what the admin wants, after

  edit, and GEN.57 says a sector depends only on the seed, the version

  GEN.57, GEN.59.

## SEC: Security

The login protection of 2026-10-01 (SEC.1, SEC.20 to
SEC.28: the always-on activity log, per-address and per-username
lockouts, trusted devices, the password blocklist and hashing cost,
two-factor sign-in and the fail2ban example) shipped in PRs #217, #220
and #221.

Design: [docs/design/operations/login-brute-force-protection.md](design/operations/login-brute-force-protection.md)

- [ ] **SEC.33 Release gate: a full security code audit of the whole code base, done before every major or minor version change (8.1 first)**
  Boss, 2026-10-21, 5:10 PM EDT: before 8.1 is stamped finished there
  must be a full security code audit, and it MUST be done before every
  single major or minor version change (8.1, 8.2 and on to 9.0 and 10.0;
  the 8.0.NNNN builds are exempt). One standing item: it stays open and
  is re-run for each major or minor version change, never retired.
  Confirmed and narrowed to this wording by Boss, 8:01 PM EDT
  2026-10-22: required whenever the major or minor number changes, not
  for build numbers. Scope: every route, API
  endpoint and form; sign-in, sessions, cookies, CSRF, rate limits and
  lockouts; authorization and every admin page; all SQL and any string
  built into a query; file, path and upload handling and the tile cache
  and jobs directory; the stored-XSS and output-escaping paths in
  templates and JavaScript; the Content-Security-Policy and headers;
  secrets, config and settings handling; the dependency list and its
  known vulnerabilities (pip and npm lockfiles); the install, update and
  deployment scripts and the systemd and Apache or nginx examples; the
  Redis and job-queue inputs; and anything new since the last pass (use
  git log since the last audited release). Run the repository's own
  static checks and add a scanner pass where one can run without the
  network. Done: for the release, a dated report
  (/mnt/project-files/reports/release-audit-security-<version>.md,
  linked from the goal issue and logged on this item as 'Release log:
  <version>, <EDT date and time>, <commit>') that names the commit
  audited, lists what was covered and what was not, and files every
  finding as its own item (a high or critical finding blocks the release
  until fixed and merged; the rest are filed with an owner). The release
  is not stamped while the report for its version is missing, or while a
  finding it marks blocking is open. Proposed owner: its own thread,
  started when the version nears close (8.1: after the whole-sphere
  audits TEST.185, TEST.184, TEST.159 and TEST.160 merge, so the audit
  sees the final code); it must not be the lane that wrote the code
  under audit.
  Ordering (TODO thread, 6:40 PM EDT 2026-10-21): this audit runs after
  the performance profile PERF.146 so it sees the final code.
  Owner: a new audit thread, started when PERF.146 closes (Boss, 7:44
  PM EDT 2026-10-22: all five cores on 8.1; this replaces any earlier
  owner line).
  Method: follow /mnt/project-files/reports/audit-playbook-2026-10-22.md
  (the coordinator, relayed 7:58 PM EDT 2026-10-22 as the lane's clock
  reads).
  Gate rule (Boss, 8:04 PM EDT 2026-10-22): the
  version is not stamped while a confirmed Critical or High finding is
  open; Mediums are filed with owners; data loss, corruption or broken
  seed reproducibility counts as High. This holds unless Boss
  specifically authorizes an exception.
  Prerequisites: none. Related: TEST.261.

## TEST: The test suite

From the test suite plan of 2026-10-01 (Boss: "build me a list of TEST
items (TEST.x) to build our testing suite to cover all edge cases, and
prepare to do another solid full on bug hunt. Don't implement just plan
for it"). Each item ends with its areas in brackets. "Suspected bug"
means read from the code, not reproduced yet; the bug hunt confirms or
clears each one.

### Infrastructure and CI

  Reported by Bugfixes lane 1 (2026-10-09 23:32Z):
  `test_ensure_sector_generated_creates_then_reuses_the_same_sector`
  failed once in a busy parallel full-suite run and passed alone, with
  no change to the code it covers. Done: the cause is found (a shared
  sector address or timing under load is the first thing to check) and

- [ ] **TEST.190 A failing session fixture makes every dependent test wait its full 900 s timeout: fail the dependents at once (bug)**
  Found by a lane (2026-10-16), filed by the TODO thread. When a
  session-scoped fixture (for example the browser-test server) fails to
  start, each test that needs it waits its whole 900 s timeout before
  failing, so one fixture failure costs hours of the run. Done: a
  fixture that fails marks its dependents as errors at once (pytest does
  that already for a raised error, so the cause is in how the fixture
  waits; find it and fix it), and a test shows a dead fixture ends the
  run in seconds. Fails on main: yes. Frequency: whenever a session
  fixture fails. Reproducer: make the server fixture raise after its
  start and time the run.
  Owner: Bug Hunt (proposed, Boss's lane started 10:20 PM EDT).
  Status (2026-10-16, 11:43 PM EDT, Bug Hunt as relayed): could not
  reproduce as described. pytest already fails the tests that depend on
  a failed session fixture at once, so the 900 s wait this item
  describes did not appear. Needed next time: The run log that shows
  dependents waiting their full timeout, and the fixture that failed
  first. Running log: the comments on issue #1694.
  Prerequisites: none. Related: TEST.111.

  central object (as binary stars are done now); every object other than
  the central object can be another system with that object as its
  central object, down to small objects that get no satellites; all
  objects follow the same physics, so the origin of the system's space

  adding a member and removing it returns the other positions exactly; a
  parent change leaves every absolute position unchanged; a sub-system's
  barycentre does not move when its members orbit; the single-member
  case equals the existing close-pair formula of `system_tree.py` bit
  for bit; and a 10 m body 10,000 AU from its parent keeps its metre in

- [ ] **TEST.244 Tests: re-primary and reparent invariants, frame round trips, momentum conservation, a moon's velocity as the sum of its hops, a locked body's rate follows a primary change**
  Part of the unified orbited-body plan (GEN.550; design note
  docs/design/architecture/unified-system-barycentre.md, decided: Boss's nine cards
  S10 to S18 on the primary-first rule, the point-in-space frames and
  motion and spin, tapped between 12:30 and 12:32 AM EDT on 2026-10-18
  (as the coordinator relayed with the wake times converted), every one
  the recommended option: S10 the original values are the origin values
  (birth mass, age, [Fe/H], composition, formation distance) plus the
  orbit-geometry draws, and the present state is recomputed about the
  new primary; S11 the heaviest is found by the total mass of each
  branch (a sub-system counts as the sum of its parts), ties under 1e-9
  relative keep the draw order; S12 when the heaviest changes in
  simulated time the step runs once at the event (merger, capture,
  ejection), state-preserving, so no body jumps; S13 trajectories are an
  analytic two-body orbit per frame with mu including the member's own
  mass, and the outer system's tide is a stability gate (Hill fraction,
  triple and Kozai screens); S14 a frame request names any of the named
  frames or any other point, found through the lowest common ancestor;
  S15 a point has a live parent link with a versioned cache and the
  copied anchors and the three `carry_*` calls go; S16 the point holds a
  kinematic record (position, velocity, spin axis and rate, mass with
  mu, epoch and next-due) with identity, radius and age beside it in the
  core; S17 spin is a unit axis plus an angular rate in rad/s; S18
  speed, axial tilt, galactic orbital period and phase, rotation period
  and a* become derived and their columns are dropped in the 8.4
  revision with DB.73). Boss's refinements of 12:23, 12:24 and 12:25 AM
  EDT, 2026-10-18 (project chat, as the coordinator relayed): any two
  objects that orbit each other follow one rule; before a system is
  validated the heaviest object becomes the primary and the others are
  recalculated from their original values; the barycentre is always the
  origin; coordinates are relative at every level, so a moon follows its
  planet and the planet follows the star; the point-in-space object
  updates the relative coordinates, knows its centre's position in wider
  space and gives converted coordinates for any frame on demand; and it
  also stores the vector of motion, the spin and the other attributes of
  the object with a mass classification. Item SY15 of the note (sections
  12.1 and 13.5). Proposed owner, not assigned by a card: Core 4, with
  GEN.576 and GEN.578. Do: tests that a pair re-primaried gives
  identical absolute positions; the step from the originals is
  idempotent and independent of the order members are listed; `reparent`
  preserves absolute position and velocity; frame round trips (body to
  planet frame to galactic and back) agree to the spacing of a double at
  the top; the mass-weighted offsets sum to zero at every level; a 10 m
  body 10,000 AU from its parent keeps its metre; total linear momentum
  and the orbital angular momentum about the barycentre are unchanged by
  `primary_first` and by `reparent`; a moon's velocity in the star's
  frame equals the sum of its hops; a locked body's rate follows a
  primary change. Do not test that the central object is the closest to
  the barycentre (it is not always: a light member on a tight orbit can
  be nearer); test that it is the heaviest. Done: all pass at several
  depths.
  Prerequisites: GEN.576, GEN.578, GEN.581, GEN.583. Related: GEN.550,
  GEN.565, GEN.576, GEN.578.

  Failure: it hit the 900 s pytest-timeout at load 10; alone it passes

  the 5 minutes alone are spent on (building the galaxy, three draws),

  times in a row at -n 4 under load. Owner: Bug Hunt (proposed by the
  TODO thread).
  Finding (Bug Hunt, relayed 10:40 AM EDT 2026-10-23 as the lane reported):
  7 s alone on its machine (the three runs of the queue take 0 s, 4 s and
  4.6 s); it does not fork, the workers are subprocesses
  (`redisqueue.RQExecutor` uses subprocess.Popen), so it is not TEST.293's
  family. Stack at the timeout (Core 5, relayed 10:45 AM EDT as the lane
  reported): the second `_run_queue(2)` was leaving its WorkQueue block,
  work.py `__exit__` -> `drain` -> `_collect(block=True)` ->
  `RQExecutor.wait` (redisqueue.py:411) in `time.sleep(POLL_SECONDS)`,
  waiting for its 2 futures, not on a Redis call; Redis was
  redis://127.0.0.1:6379/0, flushed before the gate, no stale keys; 4
  cores at load about 10 (4 xdist workers, a second 2-worker scan on
  Redis port 6390, headless Chromium at 100 to 150 percent CPU).
  Progress (Bug Hunt, #2683 merged about 1:16 PM EDT 2026-10-23 as the
  lane reported, gate green at 22,724 passed): the original hang did not
  reproduce (17 loops beside 8 CPU burners, all clean), but Core 5's
  stack fits a real gap that Bug Hunt reproduced: RQExecutor restarted a
  worker the moment it exited while tasks waited, so workers that die at
  start (an import error, out of memory, an unreachable Redis; their
  output is discarded) were started without limit (752 in 21 s). The run
  now fails after 10 workers in a row die, with the exit code and the
  command to see why. This item stays open as 'cause of the dying
  workers unknown': if it recurs, the error now names the exit code.
  Done is unchanged except that a recurrence is now diagnosable.
  Research (2026-10-09, Update): Update 1:17 AM EDT 2026-10-24 (as Core
  5 reported): the test ran `galaxy` with all stages; after PERF.123
  (#2865) `galaxy` always does every stage, so Core 5 changed
  test_parallel_generation.py to run `sectors` instead. Recheck whether
  the 900 s timeout still happens, and close this item if not. Owner:
  Bug Hunt.
  Prerequisites: none. Related: TEST.293, TEST.292, TEST.198.

## USR: User accounts

- [ ] **USR.1 User accounts**
  Boss (2026-10-01): "a full user level interface to allow users to
  bookmark this will, of course, require an email loop for password
  setting / resetting, invite only, so only an admin can invite a user
  which is done by unique link". Today there are only admin accounts:
  `admin_users`, `admin_sessions`, `admin_api_keys` and
  `admin_audit_log` in `stellarObjects/control_schema.sql`, managed by
  `stellarObjects/adminAuth.py`. Install seeds one admin with a random
  first password and `must_change_credentials`
  (`bootstrap_control_schema`), and nothing in the web interface or the
  CLI adds another account. There is no email support and no
  saved-bookmark feature (pages only have bookmarkable URLs). Order:
  USR.2, then USR.3 and USR.4, then USR.5, USR.6 and USR.7.
  Login protection already exists per username
  (`src/html/api/loginbackoff.py`, PR #131) and is planned per IP
  address (SEC.1); both must cover user logins, password resets and
  invite links too, as must SEC.20's logging and SEC.26's second
  factor.
  Research (2026-10-09, settings-seo-and-accounts.md): order stays; add
  one shared table `account_tokens` used by USR.4, USR.5 and USR.6
  (itsdangerous is not used for these tokens). The text names stale
  paths (`stellarObjects/control_schema.sql`,
  `stellarObjects/adminAuth.py`, `src/html/api/loginbackoff.py`); the
  files are now `src/planetgen/db/control_schema.sql`,
  `src/planetgen/admin/auth.py` and `src/planetgen/admin/throttle.py`
  with `api/loginguard.py`.

  Headline: 8.2 (user accounts, with sign-up by an email invitation that
  only an admin can send).
  - [ ] **USR.2 Accounts with roles: user, moderator, admin and Owner**
    Boss: "Admin can
    then make a user admin or take away admin rights on everything but the
    primary 1st admin account generated at install, that'll have a
    designation of 'Owner' and no other account can override that." Done:
    one accounts table in the control database (with an email address)
    holding a role per account (user, moderator, admin, Owner; moderator
    is stored and valid from the start, has no permissions until 10.0
    and no page assigns it, Boss 2026-10-16, 1:43 PM EDT); exactly one
    Owner,
    which is the account install creates; an admin page where admins
    promote a user to admin or demote an admin to user, refused for the
    Owner; sessions and API keys that work for every role while the
    admin-only pages and API routes stay admin-only; each role change
    written to the audit log. Question (decided below): does
    `admin_users` become
    this table (renamed, with a role column) or do users get their own
    table? Which existing account becomes Owner on a server that already
    has several admins (the lowest id?)? Can an admin demote themselves,
    or another admin? Can an admin delete or disable a user account? Do
    users get API keys?
    Research (2026-10-09, settings-seo-and-accounts.md): answer the open
    questions as in B7: one table with a role column (renamed to
    `accounts` in a follow-up; open question for Boss, default: add
    columns now); the lowest id becomes Owner; a database-level
    single-Owner unique index on a generated column; admins cannot
    demote themselves; admins disable users, only the Owner disables
    admins; delete by self or Owner; admins create API keys only at
    first. Add the console CLI `planetgen.cli.accounts
    --set-owner/--reset-password`. The control schema is the next
    Alembic revision after the current one.
    Decided (2026-10-10): Boss (19:16Z, Accept all): one accounts table
    with a role column (add the columns now, rename later); the lowest
    id is the Owner.
    Roles must fit 10.0 (roles and permissions, USR.25) without a
    rebuild: the role is one text column holding one of the four values;
    every admin-only page, route and command goes through one guard
    (`require_role`) so 10.0 swaps that single function for the
    permission check `can()` (USR.12, USR.14); no code outside that
    guard compares a role; the role change page of this item writes the
    audit row through one function that 10.0 reuses for the moderator
    role (USR.13).
    Split (2026-10-16, Boss 1:07 PM EDT: look at each item for smaller
    chunks and shared work): this item is now the umbrella and is done
    when its subitems are: DB.58, USR.26, USR.27. It mixes a
    control-database migration (role, email, status, single-Owner index
    and, per the later flows, the shared token and invite tables), the
    role model in sessions, API keys and guards (which USR.3, USR.4,
    USR.5, USR.7, USR.8 and API.6 actually wait for), an admin page and
    a console CLI.
  Decided (Boss, contradiction sweep cards, taps 6:10 to 6:12 PM EDT
  2026-10-18, as the coordinator reported them): fork 9: ADM.86 stays in
  8.1 on the Owner account stub USR.31; the full accounts of this item
  replace the stub in 8.2.

  - [ ] **USR.3 SMTP settings in the admin config**
    Boss: "We'll use SMTP for
    email which means admin config needs SMTP settings." Done: SMTP host,
    port, security (STARTTLS or TLS), username, password and From address,
    set from an admin page (and the config file/installer), with a "send
    test email" button; one small mail module that every flow in USR.4
    to USR.6 uses, which logs failures and never shows the SMTP
    password. Question (decided below): is the SMTP password kept in the
    config
    file (like the database password) or in the control database, and is
    it encrypted there? Who can change SMTP settings: any admin, or only
    the Owner? What do invites and resets do when SMTP isn't configured
    (show the link to the admin to pass on by hand?)?
    Research (2026-10-09, settings-seo-and-accounts.md): answer as in
    B9: stdlib smtplib, Owner-only (SMTP, `base_url`, From address; open
    question for Boss, default yes), password in the user's
    `config.json` (replaceable, never read back), no SMTP means invites
    show the link only; sent from an RQ job.
    Decided (2026-10-10): Boss (19:16Z, Accept all): SMTP settings are
    Owner-only; the password lives in the user's `config.json`, not the
    database.
    The SMTP form sits on the settings page of 8.1 (ADM.84) and its
    Owner-only tier is ADM.86 (Boss, 2026-10-16, 1:43 PM EDT).
    Scope after the review (2026-10-16 review): adds the smtp.* options
    (Owner tier, the password in `config.json`) to the settings model
    and builds the mail module and the "send test email" action; the
    form is the generated settings page (ADM.84 and ADM.86), not a

  - [ ] **USR.4 Invite-only sign-up by unique link**
    Boss: "only an admin can
    invite a user which is done by unique link, admin can select how many
    uses the link has or if it expires in 1 hour, 4, 6, 12, 24, 3 days, 7
    days, 1 month, 1 year, or never. Likewise invite # of uses the link
    gets can be infinite but infinite and never expire in combo ask for
    confirmation as this is not recommended." Done: an admin page that
    creates invite links (a random token stored hashed, like session
    tokens) with a use count (a number, or infinite) and one of the
    expiry choices above; infinite uses together with never expires asks
    the admin to confirm and says it isn't recommended; a list of invites
    with uses left, expiry and who made them, and a way to revoke one;
    opening a valid link lets someone register (username, email), then
    USR.5's email loop sets their password; the account is a user, not
    an admin. Question (decided below): does an admin optionally type
    the invitee's
    email so the link is sent for them, or only copy the link? Is the
    invite page rate-limited, and is there a cap on open invites? Does
    a multi-use link record who used it?
    Research (2026-10-09, settings-seo-and-accounts.md): add the
    `invite_uses` table, atomic redeem, an open-invite cap of 50 and
    rate limits (B5).
    Decided (2026-10-10): Boss (19:16Z, Accept all): invites capped at
    50 open at once; the invitee email is optional.
    Scope after the review (2026-10-16 review): the invite page (use
    count, expiry choices, confirmation for infinite plus never, the
    open-invite cap of 50, revoke, the list) and registering through a
    valid link; tokens and `invite_uses` come from the account-token
    library and the first child of USR.2. Placed after USR.5 because its
    sign-up ends in the set-password email loop.

  - [ ] **USR.5 Email loop for setting and resetting passwords**
    Boss: "an
    email loop for password setting / resetting". Done: a new account
    sets its first password from an emailed link; "forgot password" on
    the login page emails a reset link; links are single-use, short-lived
    (stored hashed) and end the account's other sessions once used; the
    page never says whether an email address has an account; resets are
    rate-limited per address and per IP alongside the existing login
    backoff and SEC.1. Question (decided below): how long a reset link
    lasts
    (30 minutes? 1 hour?); does changing the email address also need an
    email confirmation to the old and new addresses; does the Owner's
    reset need anything extra?
    Research (2026-10-09, settings-seo-and-accounts.md): lifetimes:
    reset 30 minutes, first-password 24 hours, email change 1 hour; a
    notification email on password and email change; an Owner reset asks
    for the TOTP code when enrolled.
    Decided (2026-10-10): Boss (19:16Z, Accept all): reset links last 30
    minutes, a first password link 24 hours, an email change 1 hour with
    confirmation.
    Scope after the review (2026-10-16 review): the emailed set-password
    and forgot-password flows, per-address and per-IP limits, ending
    other sessions on use; tokens come from the account-token library.
    Placed before USR.4, which needs it.

  - [ ] **USR.6 Owner transfer**
    Boss: "The owner CAN (with specific approval
    and double password confirmation and email loop confirmation) assign
    owner to someone else who then has to accept via email loop." Done:
    only the Owner can start a transfer, from a page that asks them to
    confirm the choice explicitly, enter their password twice, and then
    confirm from an email link; the chosen account then gets an email and
    must accept from its own link; only when both are done does Owner
    move; every step goes to the audit log. Question (decided below):
    what the old
    Owner becomes (admin?); does the new Owner have to be an admin
    already; how long the pending transfer lasts and whether the Owner
    can cancel it; what happens if the Owner loses their email or
    password (recovery from the server's command line?).
    Research (2026-10-09, settings-seo-and-accounts.md): the state
    machine of B10: the old Owner becomes admin; the target must be an
    admin with TOTP; it expires after 48 hours; the Owner can cancel;
    the confirm link lands on a neutral page because of
    `SameSite=Strict`.
    Decided (2026-10-10): Boss (19:16Z, Accept all): the old Owner
    becomes an admin; the target must be an admin with 2FA; a pending
    transfer expires in 48 hours.
    Scope after the review (2026-10-16 review): the Owner-transfer state
    machine and its pages; tokens come from the account-token library.

## OPS: Installers, hosting, CI, releases

OPS.1 shipped with the version scheme in `changes/README.md`.

- [ ] **OPS.55 Nightly full backup: a backup step in the daily maintenance run that takes every part into one archive, with a schedule setting and a nightly retention setting**
  Boss (2026-10-16, 2:06 PM EDT): "Yes plese." to a nightly full backup
  from the daily maintenance run. Target 8.9 (the backups and repair
  chain, umbrella ADM.91). The maintenance logic of OPS.16 (`--if-due`,
  `--only STEP`, lock, log, exit codes) gets a `backup` step that calls
  `planetgen.backup.take` of ADM.87 with every registered part
  (settings, control database ADM.88, parity data DB.40), so archives
  are taken without a click. The archive manifest carries a kind
  (`manual`, `settings-save`, `nightly`). The step is due when no
  nightly archive exists for the local day and the local hour has
  reached `settings.nightly_backup_hour` (0 to 23, default 4; the
  scheduler may call the script hourly), and it is switched off by
  `settings.nightly_backup` (default on). Nightly archives are pruned by
  their own count, `settings.nightly_backups_kept` (1 to 60, default 7),
  while `settings.backups_kept` (default 20, 1 to 200) keeps counting
  manual and settings-save archives, so a week of nightly archives never
  pushes out the archive an admin took by hand; the newest archive
  holding every part is never pruned. A failed step logs, exits non-zero
  like any other step and leaves the earlier archives alone; a run that
  finds the guard on (maintenance, an update, a run) skips and is
  retried when next due. The options go into the ADM.42 model and show
  on the settings page. Done: the step with tests for due and not due,
  off, a failure that leaves archives alone, pruning by kind, and a
  second run started during the first exiting at once; the daily run
  lists the step in its log.
  Prerequisites: ADM.88, DB.40. Related: OPS.16, ADM.87,
  ADM.91.

- [ ] **OPS.64 The version code carries the database schema, generator epoch and API versions as well**
  Asked for by Boss for 8.2. Today the version
  is MAJOR.REVISION.BUILD (for example 8.0.2040) and says nothing about
  which database schema, which generator epoch or which API version a
  build carries, so a database, a generated galaxy or a client cannot be
  matched to a release by its version alone. Make the version code carry
  all three: the database schema version (the Alembic head,
  SCHEMA_VERSION in db/store.py), the generator epoch
  (src/tests/golden/epochs.json) and the API version (API_VERSION in
  api/version.py). Decided (Boss, 12:39 AM EDT 2026-10-24, card option 1, the format is the PEP 440 local suffix): the one version string gains a PEP 440 local
  suffix that the stamping step writes, for example
  8.2.2100+db134.gen62.api5; the three numbers are read from their own
  sources at stamp time, never typed. This touches the version scheme:
  nobody hand-bumps anything, the change goes through
  scripts/bump_version.py (its stamping and its BUILD rule, where BUILD
  stays the count of stamped releases and still never resets),
  _version.py, the README badge and the CHANGELOG entry together, and
  the PR check (--check-pr) must refuse a note or file that sets the
  suffix by hand. setup.py reads __version__ by regex, so the suffix
  must stay a valid package version, and the user agent
  (util/user_agent.py) and every page or response that shows the version
  show the full code. Do:
  choose the format with Boss, teach bump_version.py to build the suffix
  from the three sources, keep its tests and --check-pr in step, and
  update changes/README.md, docs/design/architecture/design-decisions.md (the OPS.1
  version section) and the docs that quote the version format. Done: a
  stamped release carries the three numbers in its version code, they
  match the schema head, the epoch and the API version of that tree, a
  PR that edits the suffix by hand is refused, and the docs gate and the
  bump_version tests pass. Owner: none yet (pool, 8.2). Source: Boss,
  5:07 PM EDT 2026-10-23.
  Prerequisites: none. Related: OPS.56, OPS.1.

  - [ ] **VIEW.2 A starmap seen from a planet. RESEARCH WITH BOSS FIRST**
    Boss:
    "Build a function to select a planet and generate an effective starmap
    from that planet based on all visible stars, this will have to include
    a lot, A LOT, of math so remind me to do research when we get there
    into exactly how one would do that, but it would have to account for
    where each star would have been at that light years back in time?"
    Done: pick a planet (or moon), and get every star visible from it
    with its direction and brightness as seen there, placed where it was
    when the light now arriving left it (light-travel time back along
    its galactic orbit; the correlative update now moves everything along
    galactic orbits, GEN.6, PR #157). The research pass covers at least:
    - which stars are visible (apparent magnitude from luminosity and
      distance, a magnitude cut, interstellar extinction and reddening by
      dust, and whether stars beyond the generated sectors are included,
      for example from the density skeleton or the `bright_stars` table
      from PR #159);
    - star colors as seen from the planet (colour from temperature,
      reddening, the planet's atmosphere and its own star's glare; Boss
      singled out colors as needing real work);
    - light-time positions (the star's position at "now minus distance /
      c" along its galactic orbit), and where the planet is in its own
      orbit and its sky orientation (axial tilt, rotation, latitude);
    - nebulae, the galactic band, the companion stars of the planet's own
      system, and performance (millions of stars per view).
    Research (2026-10-09, sky-view.md): `bright_stars` (the 1,000 L_sun
    floor) plus the 100 ly backfill cover only about 8% to 10% of the
    naked-eye sky: a tier table (`BRIGHT_STAR_SKY_TIERS`, floors from
    visibility) or an angle-bin scatter like `scatter_layer` is needed.
    GEN.98 is built, so measure `backfill_cells` per cell on a real
    database first (the 2026-10-08 timing run measured the sector fill,
    not the backfill). Light-time: the position effect is under a tenth
    of a pixel except for hypervelocity stars; the part worth doing is
    the star's age and luminosity at the retarded time and
    supernova-remnant visibility; add the vectorised first-order
    `sky_vectors` (sky-view.md 2.2) beside VIEW.5's per-body
    `apparent_position`. GEN.104 is a prerequisite for horizon views and

    magnitude 6.5 for every planet with horizon extinction and twilight
    only; physical colour from blackbody, desaturated for faint stars,
    with a "boost colour" option; galactic plane dust A_V 1.0 per kpc;

- [ ] **POP.16 Design: settlements and nation-states on a planet with a technological civilization (the tech gate, nation count and dominance laws, the city size law, the city to nation draw, space ports), with the sources and stand-in tiers**
  Boss, 9:27 PM EDT 2026-10-24 (relayed by the coordinator): "I want to

  docs/design/habitability/settlements.md and get Boss's answers on the
  open points. It decides: (1) the tech gate, the lowest tech band at
  which a species' homeworld gets cities and nations (the Agrarian band
  of the tech table, TL 0.5 and above, is the proposal; a Primal species
  gets none) and the tech at which space ports and stations scatter
  (Atomic, TL 2.5 and above, for orbital stations; Fusion, 3.5 and
  above, for in-system ports); (2) the number of nation-states on a
  planet, drawn from the habitable land area, the species' traits and
  the tech band (a stand-in law, tier and sources named); (3) each
  nation's dominance, a power score from its land share, its population
  and the tech spread, with one or more nations flagged dominant; (4)
  the city size law for the capital and the ten largest cities
  (rank-size with a tech-limited largest city and the planet's carrying
  capacity as the cap); (5) the draw that assigns each city to a nation,
  a probability weighted by city size and nation dominance so that a
  more powerful nation tends to hold the biggest cities, the capital
  going to the dominant nation; (6) what is fixed (all of it, until 9.2)
  and which fields 9.2 will make dynamic; (7) how it composes with the
  existing species, polities and territories (a polity still owns
  systems; nations are on one planet) and with editing (8.6). Open
  points to ask Boss through the coordinator only if the research cannot
  settle them. Done: the design is in
  docs/design/habitability/settlements.md with its sources and its
  stand-in list, and every later item of this tree cites it. Owner: a
  research thread (Math 1 style) with Aux 11 for the page parts. Version
  8.2, phase 3 (the foundation). Rules for every item of this tree:
  draws go through draw.py (one named stream per draw, order fixed); a
  PR that changes drawn output carries `tests.golden_update --reason ...
  --affects population` and takes the next epoch; every number it adds
  has a unit or scale (GEN.772) and a column_units entry (new numeric
  columns in db/column_units.py); every stand-in value gets a GEN.725
  registry row with its tier and tweak labels; tests are
  `scripts/test.py changed --resume` only; no fixed content from the
  Milky Way or the Solar System.
  Prerequisites: none. Related: POP.7, POP.8, POP.9, POP.10, GEN.725,
  GEN.772.
  Research (2026-10-09, Progress): Also decides the governments rules of
  POP.25 to POP.27: the separation between homeworlds, the reach floor,
  the way chance-extra civilizations are held back, and the largest
  count a galaxy can hold.
